entities.name: SoftBank Group
entities.zh: ソフトバンクグループ
entities.desc: **OpenAI marks itself up as SoftBank's last tranche closes (#124, Sept 29-Oct 1, 2026):** OpenAI opened talks to raise at least $30B at about a $1.4T pre-money valuation, up from $852B post-money in March, after shelving its IPO. SoftBank's final $10B tranche, funded by a record high-yield bond at coupons up to 9.75%, is due October 1 and takes its commitment to about $64.6B for roughly 13%. SBG shares rose about 6% on Sept 30; SB Energy has delayed its IPO. Japan's most consequential AI investment vehicle: Vision Funds have backed 400+ technology companies globally. **AI infrastructure offensive (2025–2026):** Son has committed $500B+ in US AI infrastructure via the Stargate JV (with OpenAI, Oracle, MGX); simultaneously backing Noetra (Japan physical AI model, $6B state-backed, SoftBank consortium), SB OAI Japan GK (OpenAI exclusive Japan distribution), SB Intuitions (Japanese-language LLMs, now merged into Noetra mission), and SB Neo (US neocloud JV, Jul 2026). **ARM-SoftBank flywheel:** SoftBank's majority stake in ARM gives it unique leverage across mobile, edge, and server AI compute as the market shifts to Arm-based architectures (Apple Silicon, Nvidia Grace Hopper, AWS Graviton). The combination of AI-model bets (Noetra, SB Intuitions, SB OAI), compute bets (ARM), and infrastructure bets (Stargate) makes SoftBank the most comprehensively positioned entity in Japan's AI ecosystem. **SB Energy stake sale ahead of IPO (Aug 17, 2026):** Nvidia is investing $1.5B in SB Energy, SoftBank's US data-center developer building the 10-gigawatt Ohio campus for OpenAI, as part of a financing package that also sees Nvidia backing roughly $105B of the project's infrastructure debt (scaled back from an earlier $250B guarantee under discussion). SB Energy is targeting an IPO as soon as next month that could raise at least $5B, giving SoftBank a near-term path to monetize part of its AI-infrastructure buildout while retaining upside exposure through its remaining stake — a data point for investors tracking how SoftBank funds its OpenAI/Stargate commitments without further diluting the parent balance sheet. **Record ¥1 trillion retail bond to fund ABB robotics deal, repay OpenAI bridge loan (#85, Aug 20, 2026):** SoftBank Group finalized plans for a roughly ¥1 trillion ($6.3B) bond offering aimed at Japanese retail investors — the largest-ever retail bond sale by a Japanese company, surpassing SoftBank's own ¥600B record set in 2025 and marking its third retail bond sale this year. Seven-year notes, with a coupon expected in the upper-4% range, are earmarked for two purposes: financing the ~$5.4B acquisition of ABB's robotics division (announced Oct 2025, expected to close mid-to-late 2026) and repaying a bridge loan that backed SoftBank's stake in OpenAI. Leaning on retail debt — rather than equity monetization alone — to fund both the robotics arm of its physical-AI strategy and its OpenAI exposure underscores how central borrowed money has become to Son's AI buildout, a dynamic some analysts have flagged as a credit-strain risk if AI capex returns disappoint. **AI-native RAN validated on live 5G network (#90, Aug 20, 2026):** SoftBank Corp and Ericsson completed Japan's first live-network validation of an AI-native scheduler for link adaptation — machine-learning decisions injected directly into commercial 5G baseband equipment in real time. Results: spectral efficiency up to ~25% and downlink user throughput up to ~50% at best-performing sites, ~10% average gains across all sites tested. Distinct from SoftBank's equity-stake AI bets (Noetra, OpenAI, Stargate), this is AI built into network infrastructure SoftBank already owns — positioning ahead of 5G Advanced/6G, with monetization (licensing vs. proprietary differentiator) still an open question. Shares eased 0.56% on Aug 27 as an early Nvidia-earnings-driven rally in Tokyo chip/AI names faded into profit-taking by the close. **Record retail bond priced (#97, Sept 4, 2026):** SoftBank priced the ¥1 trillion ($6.3B) seven-year retail bond flagged on Aug 20, with the coupon set near the upper end of the previously guided 4.3–4.9% range — still Japan's largest-ever retail bond offering by any issuer. The public offering period runs Sept 7–16, with issuance Sept 17 and maturity in 2033. Proceeds remain earmarked for the ~$5.4B ABB robotics acquisition and repayment of the bridge loan behind SoftBank's OpenAI stake. The pricing is a funding-mechanics confirmation rather than a new commitment, but it is a live test of retail-investor appetite for SoftBank's AI-linked debt load at scale — a data point for the credit-strain question some analysts have raised if AI capex returns disappoint. **Record short interest collides with $25.9bn bridge-loan repayment (#105, Sept 10-15, 2026):** Short interest in SoftBank Group rose to 2.27% of float as of Sept 9 — the highest since July 2025 — with notional short value of $3.9bn, the most since S3 Partners' data began in 2015, setting up a potential short-squeeze dynamic if bearish positions are forced to cover into further rallies. The timing is pointed: SoftBank drew $30bn of a $40bn bridge facility in March to fund its OpenAI stake and is set to repay the remaining $25.9bn balance on Sept 15, with a prospective $10-20bn high-yield bond offering under consideration to refinance the facility with longer-term debt — on top of the ¥1tn retail bond and roughly $25bn already raised across bond and margin-lending markets in 2026. The convergence of record short bets, a hard Sept 15 repayment deadline, and a crowded high-yield calendar is the clearest market-structure test yet of whether SoftBank's debt-fueled AI-investment strategy (OpenAI, Stargate, ABB robotics, Noetra) can keep refinancing itself at scale without triggering the credit-strain concerns analysts have flagged since the Aug 20 retail bond. **Two-day rout on Anthropic/OpenAI AI-safety warnings, lands on bridge-loan repayment day (#108, Sept 14-15, 2026):** Shares fell as much as 13% Monday and a further 10.7% intraday Tuesday after Anthropic CEO Dario Amodei published a Sept 12 essay calling for a deliberate slowdown (減速, gensoku) in frontier AI development, a position OpenAI's Sam Altman publicly backed over the weekend along with confirming OpenAI will not IPO in 2026. The Nikkei 225 fell nearly 2% Monday and touched a six-week low near 63,000 Tuesday before closing down ~0.9% at 63,492. The reaction lands on the same day SoftBank is due to repay the $25.9bn balance of its OpenAI bridge loan — meaning an AI-safety-driven equity repricing and a hard refinancing deadline are hitting simultaneously, a pointed test of whether debt markets keep extending credit at the pace SoftBank's AI strategy requires. Morningstar's Dan Baker attributed the move to investors pricing in the chance regulators slow AI development, rather than any SoftBank-specific news. **Apollo weighs raising NAV loan to $9bn to fund OpenAI stake (#111, Sept 17, 2026):** Bloomberg reported Apollo Global Management is in talks to boost the size of a net-asset-value (NAV) loan to SoftBank's Vision Fund 2 to $9bn from $5.4bn, with the financing backed by Vision Fund 2 assets rather than SoftBank's parent balance sheet directly. Apollo first made the loan in 2021 and had already raised it by $900mn to $5.4bn last year; size and terms of the latest increase remain unfinalized, and both companies declined to comment. The talks come on top of SoftBank's already-disclosed $64.6bn OpenAI commitment and the $10bn OpenAI-holding-backed loan (including Apollo among lenders) raised in August -- meaning a fourth distinct debt instrument (NAV loan, OpenAI-holding-backed loan, ¥1tn retail bond, and the now-repaid $40bn bridge facility) is under active expansion, reinforcing the pattern of SoftBank layering multiple, differently-collateralized borrowing structures to keep funding its OpenAI/Stargate exposure rather than drawing down equity. **Record $11.15bn jumbo bond to fund third OpenAI tranche (#115, Sept 21, 2026):** SoftBank Group launched $10bn and €1.15bn (~$1.35bn) of senior unsecured notes -- split into 3.5-, 5.5- and 7.5-year dollar tranches and 4- and 6-year euro tranches -- per a term sheet circulated Sept 21. If completed at the marketed size, it would be the largest Asia-Pacific non-financial corporate bond deal on record, surpassing 7-Eleven's $10.93bn 2021 sale. Proceeds fund SoftBank's $10bn payment for the third tranche of its follow-on OpenAI investment, expected to close Oct 1, plus general corporate purposes. The deal is the fifth distinct debt instrument SoftBank has tapped in 2026 to fund its OpenAI/Stargate exposure -- after the now-repaid $40bn bridge facility, the ¥1tn retail bond, the OpenAI-holding-backed loan, and the Apollo NAV loan -- underscoring that public bond markets, not just bank and retail debt, are now absorbing SoftBank's AI-investment funding needs at record scale. **Bond priced at up to 9.75% to fund final OpenAI tranche (#121, Sept 24, 2026):** SBG priced $10bn of dollar notes (2030 8.625%, 2032 9.25%, 2034 9.75%) and EUR1bn of euro notes (7.125%, 8.0%), about JPY1.76tn in total and the largest high-yield corporate deal on record. Settlement Sept 29; proceeds fund the final OpenAI tranche due Oct 1, after which unused bridge-loan capacity is cancelled. Total OpenAI commitment reaches $64.6bn for roughly 13%. SBG has issued $14.6bn of high-yield bonds in 2026 (63% of APAC/Japan HY supply); CDS above 400bp vs ~280bp in June; shares fell 3.2% on Sept 25 while the Nikkei rose. **SAIMEMORY picks Shinko for ZAM packaging (#123, Sept 28, 2026):** SoftBank's memory subsidiary signed a basic agreement with Shinko Electric Industries to develop packaging and manufacturing processes for Z-Angle Memory, its Intel-based HBM alternative; prototypes FY2027, practical use FY2029.

entities.name: NEC Corporation
entities.desc: Japan's leading enterprise IT services provider with deep government relationships. NEC's AI portfolio spans facial recognition (ranked #1 globally by NIST FRVT for several years), natural language processing, and digital twin platforms. **'Corporate AI & Workforce Division': first all-AI department (#83, Aug 10, 2026):** NEC announced it had formally established a new department, effective Aug 1, in which every role from division head to staff is filled by an AI agent rather than a human. Seventeen named AI agents — organized into four tiers (AI Division Head, AI Board, AI Managers, AI Employees) — handle tasks like sales-dashboard updates and extracting action items from meeting minutes, and can autonomously spin up new AI agents to respond to requests from other departments; humans retain final decision-making, quality control, and performance evaluation. **ITU-T standardizes AI-era network framework (#84, Aug 21, 2026):** NEC, alongside NTT, KDDI, Fujitsu subsidiary 1Finity, Rakuten Mobile, Oki Electric, and Sumitomo Electric, announced that the ITU-T (International Telecommunication Union) approved as Recommendation Y.3335 a framework the seven companies co-developed for low-latency, energy-efficient network paths across different operators — a technical building block for the All-Photonics Network (APN) that Japan's Beyond 5G/6G strategy positions as core infrastructure for physical AI (robotics, remote sensor processing). The standard, approved Aug 13 and announced Aug 21, gives NEC and its telecom-equipment peers an early lead in exporting Japan-originated network architecture as a global standard ahead of a follow-on ITU-T functional-architecture Recommendation targeted for October 2028. **Anthropic camp / 'Japanese-style AI' (Aug 14, 2026):** Nikkei Asia reported NEC, alongside Fujitsu and Hitachi, is partnering with Anthropic to promote a security- and reliability-first AI development posture for critical infrastructure and government systems — a distinct competitive camp from the NTT Data/SoftBank-OpenAI push toward scale and innovation, as Japan's top IT firms target a shift to AI-led software development by 2030. **MHI defense/AI-sovereignty strategic alliance MOU (#99, Sept 2, 2026):** NEC and Mitsubishi Heavy Industries signed an MOU for a strategic partnership in the defense sector, agreeing to deepen collaboration on operation plans, command-and-control systems, and unmanned assets, with the explicit stated goal of reinforcing Japan's industrial base for defense and establishing 'data and AI sovereignty.' NEC President Takayuki Morita framed it as a step toward 'a truly sovereign and highly reliable defense system' combining Japan's technologies and domain expertise; MHI's Eisaku Ito used identical sovereignty language. The deal extends NEC's government-facing AI portfolio (already spanning facial recognition, the all-AI Corporate AI & Workforce Division, and the ITU-T Y.3335 network standard) into defense command-and-control — a segment where AI-assisted decision systems for unmanned assets are becoming a core national-security procurement category as Japan's Ministry of Defense modernizes. **Kotoba-1 (Japanese LLM):** Developed with NVIDIA as part of Japan's domestic LLM push. Part of the Noetra consortium (SoftBank, Sony, Honda, NEC) — contributing large-scale model training expertise and enterprise distribution.

entities.name: Fujitsu
entities.desc: Japan's largest IT services company, repositioning from labor-intensive systems integration toward AI infrastructure and AI-augmented services. **MONAKA CPU goes on sale globally (#110, Sept 14, 2026):** standalone sales of the 144-core, Arm-based, 3D-stacked MONAKA CPU and MONAKA servers start November 2026, shipments from April 2027; dies are made at TSMC today, with Rapidus flagged as the future domestic source (Hot Chips disclosure, #89). Shares rose 5% on the announcement. **Active cyber defense as a service line (#91 Aug 26; #122 Sept 25, 2026):** after setting out an AI-era cyber strategy built on a 'Cyber Security Nerve Center', AI Threat Hunting and its Takane LLM, Fujitsu launched a packaged service on Sept 25 combining dark-web monitoring (via Israel's KELA under an MSSP/reseller deal), attack surface management and Red Team-led threat hunting for critical-infrastructure operators, days before Japan's Active Cyber Defense law lets police and the SDF neutralize attack servers from Oct 1. The Nerve Center goes live in October. **Physical AI platform (Aug 13, 2026):** systems-integrator role in the Nvidia platform with Fanuc, Yaskawa and Kawasaki Heavy.

entities.name: Sony AI
entities.desc: Sony's dedicated AI research arm, positioned at the intersection of AI and creative industries. **GT Sophy:** AI agent that defeated professional esports drivers in Gran Turismo at superhuman level (Nature paper, 2022) — one of the highest-profile real-world AI sports victories. **AI imaging:** Sony's CMOS image sensors (70%+ global market share) are the primary data input for vision-AI systems globally; Sony AI is developing neural image processing that keeps sensor and AI model development tightly linked. **Noetra consortium:** Sony is a founding investor in Noetra alongside SoftBank, NEC, and Honda — contributing its sensor/imaging data infrastructure and entertainment AI expertise to Japan's sovereign physical-AI foundation model initiative.

entities.bio: Founded April 2020, Tokyo and Zurich, as a dedicated AI research subsidiary of Sony Group Corporation (founded 1946 by Masaru Ibuka and Akio Morita, listed TSE 6758 / NYSE SONY). President: Hiroaki Kitano, a pioneering AI researcher also known for RoboCup co-founding. Focuses on AI for entertainment, gaming, imaging, and creative industries.

entities.name: Preferred Networks (PFN)
entities.zh: プリファードネットワークス
entities.desc: Japan's most credible domestic deep learning lab with a hardware-software integration thesis. **MN-Core chip series:** Japan's first proprietary neural network accelerator chip (MN-Core 1, MN-Core 2 in production) — a bet that competitive AI requires owning the full compute stack, made years before the AI chip race became a mainstream thesis. **PLaMo LLM:** Japanese-language foundation model built for enterprise use. **Industrial clients:** Toyota (automated logistics, quality inspection), Fanuc (AI-powered CNC and industrial robot vision), NTT — all cornerstone investors. **RIKEN collaboration:** Co-developing next-generation deep learning frameworks with Japan's premier AI research institution. PFN occupies a unique position in Japan's AI ecosystem: it is simultaneously a chipmaker, a model lab, and an industrial automation company — a vertical integration rare for a private firm of its size. **IPO plans to fund MN-Core mass production (#102, Sept 9, 2026):** Bloomberg and The Japan Times reported PFN is targeting an IPO window of 2028–2030 to fund mass production of its MN-Core AI chips, which the company says can run generative-AI workloads up to 10x faster than conventional Nvidia GPUs. Chip samples are due to customers in H1 2027, with a commercial launch to corporate clients at home and abroad slated for December 2027; TSMC and Samsung handle fabrication, and backers now include Toyota, SBI Group, Fanuc, and NTT. The move underscores how far up the capital-intensity curve independent AI chip design has moved — even Japan's most credible domestic model-and-chip lab increasingly needs public-market capital, not just corporate-venture backing, to compete at foundry scale. **Mitsubishi Heavy Industries capital alliance (#114, Sept 16, 2026):** MHI is investing ¥10 billion in PFN through a third-party share allotment, converting the two companies' June 2026 business tie-up into a formal capital and business alliance. The partnership targets AI for the intelligence and autonomy of machinery and systems in mission-critical applications — social infrastructure and national-security-adjacent domains — giving PFN a heavy-industry balance sheet and deployment channel distinct from its existing Toyota/Fanuc/NTT industrial-automation base, at the same time PFN is separately courting public markets to fund MN-Core chip production. **MN-Core 2 goes live inside Matlantis (#116, Sept 18, 2026):** PFN and PFCI announced MN-Core 2 will become a selectable compute option inside Matlantis, PFN's commercial atomistic-materials simulator used by 150+ companies and research institutions, delivering up to 4x the speed of GPUs on tasks like crystal-structure calculations without requiring users to change their workflow. This is PFN's first deployment of MN-Core 2 inside a live commercial product with an existing paying customer base, rather than an internal or lab benchmark — a more concrete data point for the 2028-2030 IPO thesis built around MN-Core mass production than test results alone.

entities.name: NTT Research
entities.desc: Long-horizon fundamental research division of NTT Group, focused on physics-inspired AI, cryptography, and quantum computing. **Coherent Ising Machine (CIM):** NTT Research pioneered the CIM — a photonic computing approach that converts combinatorial optimization problems into laser oscillator networks, potentially solving problems that are intractable for classical computers. Key partnership: Stanford University (YAQU quantum computing center). NTT Research's mandate is to make bets 5–20 years out rather than optimize for near-term product cycles — an unusual posture in Japan's corporate R&D landscape that is increasingly valued as the AI research horizon extends.
entities.bio: NTT Research, Inc. (founded 2019, Sunnyvale CA) is the global research arm of Nippon Telegraph and Telephone Corporation (NTT), Japan's largest telecoms company (founded 1985, listed TSE 9432; market cap ~¥14T). Focuses on fundamental research in physics, cryptography, and AI that may take 5–20 years to commercialize.

entities.name: NTT Corporation
entities.desc: Japan's largest telecoms company and parent of the NTT Group, distinct here from its NTT Research (fundamental physics/crypto R&D) and NTT Data (IT services/systems integration) subsidiaries tracked separately in this landscape — this entry covers the parent's core commercial network-infrastructure business, centered on IOWN (Innovative Optical and Wireless Network, 革新的光無線ネットワーク), NTT's next-generation all-optical computing and communications architecture. **IOWN/APN adopted for AI-enabled SDF command network (#94, Aug 30, 2026):** Nikkei reported Japan's Ministry of Defense will adopt IOWN's All-Photonic Network (APN, オールフォトニクス・ネットワーク) as the core transport layer connecting Self-Defense Forces units and bases nationwide, carrying radar, sensor, and drone data to command centers and data centers for AI-assisted analysis. The adoption will be written into the next National Defense Program Guidelines, with related costs folded into the FY2027 defense budget request and full-scale operation targeted from FY2028 — a significant government-infrastructure win for IOWN commercialization. NTT shares rose on the report. **ITU-T APN standardization:** NTT co-developed, with NEC, KDDI, and others, the ITU-T Y.3335 framework for low-latency, energy-efficient cross-operator network paths — a technical building block for APN as Japan's Beyond 5G/6G strategy positions it as core infrastructure for physical AI (robotics, remote sensor processing).

entities.name: Noetra (Japan AI Foundation Model Development Co.)
entities.zh: 日本AIファウンデーションモデル開発 / Noetra
entities.desc: Japan's state-backed foundation-model company, renamed from Japan AI Foundation Model Development on June 1, 2026 and operating since July 1. **Know-how strategy (#129, Oct 5, 2026):** President Hironobu Tamba opened Nikkei's GenAI/SUM 2026 arguing that operational know-how held by Japanese companies is Japan's winning path in AI. Noetra is building a multimodal 'mothership' model covering language, image, audio, video, sensor data and a world model, from which members will distill smaller task models; open weights are planned. Tamba says reliance on foreign models risks being cut off and that second-tier models give second-tier results. **Funding and coalition:** METI allocated ¥387.3bn for FY2026, with up to about ¥1tn over FY2026-2030 subject to annual stage-gate reviews. Shareholders number 44, led by SoftBank, NEC, Sony Group and Honda plus the three megabanks and Nippon Steel; about 28 are manufacturers. Large multimodal model targeted by 2028, commercial deployment around 2030. Risk: the data edge depends on competing shareholders actually sharing process data, and the first stage-gate review comes before any model ships.

entities.bio: Founded 2026, Tokyo, by a consortium of SoftBank, Sony, NEC, and Honda; CEO: Hironobu Tamba (also former CEO of SB Intuitions until February 2026). Japan's state-backed physical AI foundation model initiative, supported by approximately $6B in government funding under METI's AI framework. Mission: develop Japan's sovereign large-scale physical AI model — a Japan-specific LLM with robotics/embodied AI capabilities.

entities.name: Rapidus
entities.desc: Japan's state-backed attempt to make 2nm logic at home, using IBM-licensed gate-all-around technology at its IIM-1 fab in Chitose, Hokkaido. **Customer push: Rapidus CORE (#129, Oct 5, 2026):** Rapidus launched the Collaborative Open Rapid Ecosystem and, as its first phase, signed 17 Design Solution Associates (Synopsys, Cadence, Dai Nippon Printing, TOPPAN, Toshiba Information Systems, NSW, Infosys, Wipro, HCL, MosChip, Quest Global, SkyeChip, Oppstar, Infinecs, AION Silicon, GreatAsic, MavissDesign) to do design work for prospective customers and route them to the fab. EDA and IP categories come next. The move targets the company's binding constraint: no volume customer has been named, and a 2nm design costs roughly 15x a 28nm one. **Schedule and capacity:** CEO Atsuyoshi Koike has reaffirmed volume 2nm production in H2 FY2027, with about 6,000 wafer starts a month initially rising toward 25,000 by 2028 and 1.4nm development aimed at 2029. Profitability is targeted around FY2030 and an IPO around FY2031. **Funding dependence:** METI filed another ¥150bn capital request in the FY2027 budget (Sept 1, 2026) after a ¥150bn government round in June; cumulative state support approved is reported near ¥3tn against total investment needs above ¥7tn. Banks want a larger equity cushion before lending, so Rapidus still relies on repeated public injections.
entities.bio: Founded August 2022, Tokyo, by a consortium of eight major Japanese companies (Toyota, NTT, Sony, Softbank, Kioxia, Denso, NEC, and MUFG) with METI backing. CEO: Atsuyoshi Koike (formerly of Western Digital Japan). IBM technology partnership for 2nm process. Mission: manufacture 2nm chips in Japan by 2027.

entities.name: TSMC JASM (Kumamoto)
entities.desc: Japan's most significant semiconductor manufacturing investment in decades. **Fab 1 (operational Feb 2024):** 12nm and 16nm nodes for Sony CMOS image sensors and automotive/industrial chips; 50,000 wafers/month capacity. $8.6B total investment; received ¥476B ($3.2B) in METI subsidies — the largest single-project Japanese semiconductor subsidy ever. **Fab 2 (announced Feb 2024, upgraded to 3nm in 2026):** originally 6nm with ¥732B ($5B) METI subsidy; TSMC said in February 2026 it would make 3nm chips there, Taiwan approved the upgrade March 31, and reports put capacity near 15,000 wafers/month with mass production in 2028. **Fab 3 (under consideration):** Sub-2nm process with Arm partnership. **'Silicon Island' Taiwan-Japan supply chain deepens (#92, Aug 24-25, 2026):** Nikkei reported ITOCHU Techno-Solutions (CTC) formed an IT joint venture with Taiwan's Systex in Fukuoka to help Taiwanese suppliers set up operations near JASM, part of a broader wave — Taiwan-to-Japan direct investment approvals rose from 99 cases (2024) to a record 128 (2025). The buildout is backed by a government-and-industry pledge of ¥68 trillion (~$450B) in cumulative semiconductor investment through 2040, and a 'Kumamoto Science Park' modeled on Taiwan's Hsinchu Science Park is under construction alongside the existing Sony/TEL cluster. Regional impact: Kumamoto has transformed into Japan's fastest-growing semiconductor ecosystem hub ('Silicon Island Kyushu') — drawing 800+ supply-chain companies; 40K+ direct and indirect jobs; housing prices +30–50%; university enrollment growth. TSMC's decision to locate in Japan is a geopolitical endorsement: Japan provides a stable, allied manufacturing base outside Taiwan, and Taipei's Chung-Hua Institution for Economic Research has explicitly framed the deepening tie-up as building supply-chain resilience within the 'democratic camp.' **Parent TSMC posts a second straight record month (#106, Sept 10-11, 2026):** TSMC's August revenue hit a record NT$514.8B, up 53.3% y/y and 10.1% above July's already-record NT$467.58B -- the second consecutive all-time monthly high, with January-August cumulative revenue up 39.3% y/y. Management guides Q3 growth of 46.8% and record FY2026 capex of $60-64B, with orders from AI-infrastructure buildout now outpacing the company's own construction of new capacity. The read-through for JASM Kumamoto is indirect but real: a parent running above its own capacity-build pace is the demand backdrop against which JASM's Fab 2 (6nm, targeted 2027) and any Fab 3 decision get made, and it reinforces the case for the Kumamoto equipment-and-materials cluster (TEL, Sony, Denso) that has built up around the fab. **Air Liquide commits €170M+ to a Kyushu logic expansion (#128, Sept 30, 2026):** Air Liquide will build, own and operate ultra-high-purity nitrogen, oxygen, argon and hydrogen units with large backup storage for an unnamed leading chipmaker's logic expansion in southern Japan, under a long-term contract. The description fits JASM's second fab, though neither company named the customer. Gas plants are contracted well before tool move-in, so the order is a sign the 3nm schedule is being built out.

Fab 1 started volume production in February 2024 (12nm/16nm processes). JASM is majority-owned by TSMC (86.5%), with Sony Semiconductor Solutions (6.2%), Denso (6.2%), and Toyota (1.5%) as Japanese minority investors. CEO: Taiji Sakai.

entities.name: Sony-TSMC Image Sensor JV (Kumamoto)
entities.zh: ソニー・TSMC 新会社（熊本）
entities.desc: Ensures Sony's CMOS image sensor supply chain remains in Japan and on TSMC's leading-edge process nodes, giving Sony supply security for its dominant global imaging position. Sony's image sensors are used in virtually all smartphones (Apple, Samsung, Google), automotive cameras, and industrial vision systems — making this Kumamoto capacity a critical supply-chain chokepoint for global consumer electronics. The investment also ensures TSMC's Kumamoto facility has anchor demand from a premium Japanese customer, de-risking the fab's utilization during ramp. **Definitive agreement signed (Aug 11, 2026):** Sony Semiconductor Solutions and TSMC signed a legally binding agreement to form Advanced Vision Semiconductor Manufacturing Corporation, based in Koshi City, Kumamoto Prefecture, converting the Aug 10 framework into a formal joint venture roughly five months ahead of the previously targeted Mar 2027 formalization date. Sony holds 62% and TSMC 38% of the ¥747B (~$4.7B) venture — a refinement of the initially reported 60/40 split and ¥1T figure. Sony leads core sensor technology and product design while TSMC supplies the advanced process technology; mass production remains targeted for 2029.

Not a standalone JV company — Sony is a 6.2% equity investor in JASM and has reserved dedicated capacity for imaging sensor wafers.

entities.name: Kioxia
entities.desc: **Joins Applied Materials' EPIC Center (#125, Sept 29, 2026):** Kioxia became the fourth major memory maker, after Samsung, SK hynix and Micron, inside Applied's $5bn Silicon Valley equipment and process R&D hub, co-developing stacked-die memory architectures, multi-die interconnect and the dielectric, metal-fill and etch materials needed to push 3D NAND from ~332 layers toward 500+; its CBA (CMOS bonded to array) wafer-bonding design is the base. Shares +5.55% on Oct 1, the first day after the 3-for-1 split, as Micron's results (Q1 guide $61.5bn, LTAs $32bn) lifted Tokyo chip stocks. Tokyo Electron, Applied's main NAND etch/deposition rival, is the exposed supplier as Kioxia tools its next Iwate fab. Japan's — and the world's — legacy NAND flash memory champion, now navigating the transition from AI-driven hypergrowth to signs of moderating momentum. **NAND supercycle drove record but merely mediocre results:** Q1 FY2026 (quarter to June) operating profit hit a record ¥1.326tn on 415% YoY revenue growth to ¥1.767tn — but both figures missed Bloomberg consensus, and shares initially sold off, as investors read the miss as an early signal that the extraordinary AI-driven NAND price surge of 2025–26 may be cresting. **Capital-return pivot:** Alongside the print, Kioxia announced a 3-for-1 stock split (effective October 1, record date September 30) to broaden its investor base, plus an up-to-¥800bn share buyback (roughly 5.5% of shares outstanding) running August 3 through October 30 — part of a broader 50% total-shareholder-return commitment, with the company's first-ever dividend slated for fiscal 2028. **Western Digital partnership and origin:** The long-running WD joint venture at Yokkaichi and Kitakami (Iwate) remains central to Kioxia's manufacturing base, even as WD's proposed Sandisk NAND spin-off adds uncertainty to the alliance's future terms; Kioxia's own history — spun out of Toshiba's flash memory unit after the Westinghouse nuclear crisis forced a sale — remains the cautionary backdrop to how the company thinks about capital discipline today. **Nvidia-beat rally, then fade (#90, Aug 27, 2026):** Shares jumped as much as 6% through ¥50,000 in early Tokyo trade after Nvidia's blowout Q2 print (data-center revenue +117% YoY to $89bn), part of a broader chip-stock rally that faded into profit-taking by the close — a reminder of how tightly Kioxia now trades on AI-capex sentiment out of the US. **Third Iwate fab: ¥1tn ($6.3bn) Fab3 at Kitakami (#91, Aug 27, 2026):** Kioxia announced plans to build a third production building, Fab3, at its Kitakami plant in Iwate Prefecture, with total investment expected to top ¥1tn ($6.3bn) — its largest single capacity commitment since Fab2 began operating in 2025. Fab3 will be built with manufacturing partner SanDisk (successor to the original Western Digital joint venture) and will produce next-generation high-density 3D flash memory aimed at AI-driven data-center and enterprise-storage demand; operations are targeted for fiscal 2029. Kioxia and SanDisk plan to apply for Japanese government subsidies, continuing METI's pattern of underwriting domestic memory capacity (as with TEL, TSMC JASM, and Rapidus) — a signal that Japan's semiconductor industrial policy is now extending its capital-intensity bet from logic and equipment into NAND flash at the same moment Kioxia's own Q1 results suggested the 2025-26 AI-driven NAND price supercycle may be cresting. **Aggregate $31bn (¥5tn) Japan investment plan through 2032, contingent on government support (#99, Aug 27, 2026):** Kioxia and Sandisk formally announced anticipated combined investments exceeding $31bn across both the Yokkaichi and Kitakami plants through 2032 — the umbrella figure covering the Fab3 Kitakami commitment already tracked above. The companies noted the joint venture has invested over $50bn (~¥9tn) in Japan over the past 25 years, and framed the new spending as 'aligned with economic policy goals' of the Takaichi administration — explicit political positioning alongside the commercial rationale (AI-driven bit-demand growth) for the capacity build. **CEO rules out deeper SK Hynix tie-up, pledges to manage NAND price rises (#107, Sept 9, 2026):** Bloomberg reported Kioxia's chief executive dismissed the prospect of a closer partnership with SK Hynix -- which holds an indirect stake in Kioxia via a Bain Capital-linked investment vehicle -- while committing to manage further memory-price increases so they do not choke off long-term AI-linked demand, even as NAND and DRAM makers across the sector pursue costly capacity expansion to meet price rises that have run into double and triple digits on some parts. The comments are a distinct data point from Kioxia's own Aug 27 capacity announcements (the $31bn/¥5tn Japan investment plan and the ¥1tn Fab3 at Kitakami): those were supply-side commitments, while this is demand-management messaging aimed at preventing the current NAND supercycle from pricing out the AI-infrastructure buyers driving it. The muted market reaction suggests investors are treating it as expected positioning rather than new information, but it is a marker worth tracking against Kioxia's Q2 FY2026 print (due later in the fall) for whether pricing discipline shows up in realized ASPs. **Steepest decline in the memory/equipment complex on AI-safety selloff (#108, Sept 14, 2026):** Kioxia fell 8.6% Monday, the largest single-day drop among Japan's AI-linked chip names, as Anthropic/OpenAI AI-safety warnings triggered a broad risk-off in AI-capex-sensitive stocks (see SoftBank, Tokyo Electron, Advantest). Kioxia's shares have shown outsized volatility since July on both good and bad AI-sentiment days, consistent with its role as a high-beta gauge of AI server and data-center memory demand rather than a reaction to anything specific to its own NAND pricing or capacity plans. **Exploring a $10bn+ US ADR listing for spring 2027 (#111, Sept 14-15, 2026):** Bloomberg reported Kioxia is in talks with Bank of America, Goldman Sachs, and JPMorgan about listing American Depositary Shares on a US exchange, seeking to raise at least $10bn as early as spring 2027. Kioxia confirmed it is 'preparing' an ADS listing to 'steadily and sustainably increase corporate value,' while stressing schedule and structure remain undecided. The strategic logic is distinct from Kioxia's Aug 27 capacity announcements (the $31bn Japan investment plan, Fab3 Kitakami): a US listing would deepen dollar liquidity after the company's large domestic buyback program, and could open the door to inclusion in US semiconductor indices -- a different lever from the supply-side capacity bet, aimed at the investor-base side of the AI-memory-supercycle story. Shares have continued to trade as a high-beta AI proxy in the days since, with a broader Japan chip-stock roundup on Sept 17 noting Kioxia's revenue path (¥1.08T FY2024 to a projected ¥2.34T FY2026) and its +386.6% year-to-date return as the backdrop against which the ADR plan is being read. **NAND controllers start becoming AI compute layers, not just storage (#115, Sept 9-22, 2026):** TrendForce's Sept 9 NAND Flash Market Bulletin flagged a structural shift distinct from the pricing and listing narratives already tracked above: under Nvidia's new CMX architecture, NAND controllers are being redesigned to offload KV-cache management, CXL communication, and data compression -- tasks that used to sit exclusively on CPUs and GPUs -- turning SSDs from passive storage into active participants in AI inference pipelines. TrendForce frames this as a three-phase roadmap: near-term cache offloading to ease HBM/DRAM capacity constraints, mid-term dedicated low-latency near-memory computing, and long-term 3D heterogeneous integration of NAND and AI compute chips. For Kioxia, running its Yokkaichi and Kitakami fabs at full capacity with 2026 output already sold out, the shift changes what customers are ultimately paying for -- a controller that offloads AI workloads commands a different margin profile than commodity storage, giving Kioxia and its controller-design partners a multi-year window to build that positioning before it commoditizes in turn. **CEO caps data-center pricing, cites 'cloud budgets are not infinite' (#119, Sept 24, 2026):** Kioxia CEO Hiroo Ota told his sales team to stop pushing further NAND price increases to data-center customers, prioritizing multi-year customer relationships over near-term margin even as NAND prices have already risen over 100% in Q1 2026 and another 70% in Q2, with Kioxia's operating margin at 40.66%. The stance diverges from SK Hynix and Micron, both still raising prices into the same supply squeeze. Kioxia debuted new EXCERIA PRO G2 (14,900 MB/s) and EXCERIA G3 (10,000 MB/s) consumer NVMe drives at Tokyo Game Show 2026, and on Sept 15 formally confirmed -- via a notice addressing media speculation -- that it is preparing a US ADS listing while stressing timing, venue, and structure remain undecided, a continuation of the Sept 14-15 reporting already tracked above.

entities.name: Tokyo Electron (TEL)
entities.desc: **CFO points to a record ¥1tn operating profit (#132, Oct 6, 2026):** CFO Hiroshi Kawamoto (川本弘) told Nikkei Asia that operating profit should rise about 60% to a record ¥1tn in the year to March 2027, helped by price increases as well as volume. H1 guidance was raised on Jul 30 to ¥1.62tn sales and ¥458bn operating profit; TEL sees wafer-fab equipment spending above $150bn in 2026 and $190bn in 2027, and targets a 50% gross margin early in FY3/2028. Shares fell 2.38% on Oct 7 as the TELWY ADR split took effect; Q2 results are due Oct 30. **SEAJ: August Japan-made tool sales hit a record (#127, late Sept 2026):** Japan-made chip equipment sales (3-month average) reached ¥597.9bn in August, +47.4% y/y and +7.5% m/m, the highest monthly figure since records began in 1986 and the eighth straight y/y gain, driven by HBM/DRAM and TSMC advanced-logic spending. SEAJ's July forecast sees FY2026 at ¥6.55tn (+26%), FY2027 ¥7.40tn (+13%), FY2028 ¥7.77tn (+5%). TEL is the largest contributor to the series. Japan's semiconductor equipment bellwether and the world's #3 equipment maker — a critical node in the global fab supply chain. **Record FY2026 results, FY2027 H1 guidance beats consensus by 33% YoY (#101, Sept 7, 2026):** TEL's FY2026 net sales hit a record ¥2.443 trillion ($15.7B) at a 25.6% operating margin; FY2027 first-half guidance of ¥1.57 trillion (33% above the prior-year period) came in well ahead of the ¥1.42 trillion analyst consensus. TEL is investing ¥104 billion ($667M) in a new production building at its Miyagi Prefecture facility for plasma-etch and other equipment, due for completion in 2027 — management's clearest capital-allocation signal yet that it views the current AI-driven demand cycle as structural rather than transitory. The company's five largest customers (TSMC, Samsung, Intel, SK Hynix, Micron) represent roughly 55% of revenue, all mid-expansion for AI capacity; China has fallen to ~35% of revenue from a FY2024 peak of ~42% as export-control scope widens. The guidance beat is also cited (via Japan's Cabinet Office Business Conditions Index, which logged a fourth consecutive 'Improving' reading in July 2026 on the back of semiconductor-equipment order flow) as a direct structural input into Japan's national growth statistics — and, via that same BCI print, into the case for a BOJ rate hike at the Sept 17-18 meeting. **Third round of export controls takes effect (Aug 1, 2026):** METI's May 29, 2026 revision to the FEFTA control list added, for the first time, complete equipment for the entire advanced-packaging chain — not just front-end wafer fabrication tools — effective August 1. This is the third major tightening since the original July 2023 controls and directly targets the CoWoS/SoIC-style advanced packaging China's fabs need to compensate for restricted access to leading-edge lithography. TEL, along with Screen Holdings, Disco, and Kokusai Electric, already saw China sales fall sharply after the first two rounds; the new packaging-equipment scope closes off one of the remaining channels Chinese customers had been using to backfill capability, but China still accounted for roughly a third of TEL's revenue as of FY2024, so the move cuts both ways — squeezing a major customer base even as it protects the technology gap Japan's equipment makers rely on for pricing power elsewhere. **AI capex beneficiary:** Each generation of leading-edge AI training chip (TSMC N3/N2/A16, Samsung SF2) requires new TEL etch and deposition equipment purchases. TSMC's Kumamoto Fab 1 and 2 are direct TEL revenue events. **HBM equipment:** High Bandwidth Memory production requires specialized thermal processing equipment where TEL has strong positioning — a structural tailwind from AI chip demand for HBM stacks. **Order-book confirmation via Reuters Tankan (#81, Aug 11-12 2026):** The monthly Reuters Tankan survey (fielded Jul 29–Aug 6) showed Japan's manufacturer sentiment index climbing to +18 in August from +13 — the highest since March — driven almost entirely by semiconductor-linked demand: the chemicals sub-index jumped to +33 from +23 and metal/machinery to +25 from +12. A precision-machinery respondent reported receiving 'twice the normal volume of orders, an unprecedented situation.' It's independent, forward-looking confirmation of the same AI-capex order flow TEL has been citing in guidance. **Nikkei selloff on Hormuz oil risk (Aug 18 2026):** TEL shares fell 2.9% as the Nikkei dropped 1.6% to 68,098.54 after a US-Iran ceasefire lapsed and crude spiked on renewed Strait of Hormuz disruption, pushing the 10-year JGB yield to a fresh three-decade high near 2.95% — a reminder that TEL's valuation remains sensitive to macro/rate swings even as underlying chip-equipment demand strengthens. **Repeat selloff as JGB yield tops 3% (#95, Sept 1, 2026):** TEL fell 3.4%, the single biggest drag on the Nikkei 225, as the 10-year JGB yield pushed above 3% for the first time since 1996 and renewed Middle East-linked oil gains revived the same inflation/rate-discounting dynamic that hit the stock on Aug 18. Advantest fell 1.6% alongside it. The move is a valuation story rather than a demand story — nothing in TEL's underlying order book has changed since its record Q1 FY2027 guidance (Jul 30) or the Aug 12 Reuters Tankan confirmation of AI-linked capex strength — but it underscores that TEL's re-rating over 2026 has made the stock a high-beta proxy for JGB yield moves, not just chip-cycle sentiment. **September Reuters Tankan: electronics sentiment hits a new high (#104, Sept 9, 2026):** The Reuters Tankan poll (fielded Aug 26-Sept 4) showed the manufacturer sentiment index at +21, its highest since December 2021, with the electronics sub-index -- the one most directly tied to TEL's customer base -- surging to +39 from +24 the prior month on AI-linked semiconductor and data-center demand. It's the third consecutive monthly Reuters Tankan reading (following Aug 12's +18) confirming the same order-flow strength TEL has been citing in its own guidance, this time from an independent survey rather than TEL's internal numbers. **Two-day slide as AI-safety warnings compound oil-driven rate jitters (#108, Sept 14-15, 2026):** TEL fell 2.6% Monday and a further 1% Tuesday as Anthropic/OpenAI AI-safety warnings (see SoftBank) and a fresh oil-price jump after Saudi Arabia shut a major pipeline revived the same inflation/rate-discounting dynamic that hit the stock on Aug 18 and Sept 1. Nothing in TEL's own order book changed — the move sits against, not on top of, the Sept 7 guidance beat and the Sept 9 Reuters Tankan record — but it is a fresh instance of the stock trading as a high-beta proxy for both global AI-capex sentiment and JGB-yield moves simultaneously, two external variables converging in the same week as the Sept 17-18 BOJ meeting. **Bengaluru India R&D site announced (Sept 19, 2026):** TEL is opening a software-development site in Bengaluru focused on equipment design and simulation, and plans joint research with Indian universities on next-generation semiconductor technologies — part of a broader wave of Japanese materials/equipment firms (Fujifilm, Sumitomo Chemical, Hirata) deepening ties with India's semiconductor buildout at Semicon India 2026. This is R&D/software work, not a manufacturing shift, and sits alongside (not in place of) TEL's ¥104bn Miyagi production-building expansion. **Gujarat semiconductor training center backed by METI (#114, Sept 19-20, 2026):** At Semicon India 2026, Tokyo Electron confirmed plans to open a dedicated semiconductor training center in Gujarat in 2027 to build a fab- and equipment-engineer talent pipeline for India's expanding chip industry, under a METI-selected HR-development-ecosystem project distinct from the software-and-simulation R&D site TEL is separately opening in Bengaluru (#113). The training center is a government-cost-shared workforce play rather than a capacity or revenue commitment — TEL's return is a trained local labor pool and preferred-vendor positioning as India's incentive-backed fabs (Tata Electronics' Dholera plant among them) move from construction to hiring, a slower-moving but genuinely incremental variable layered on top of the Bengaluru R&D site and the ¥104bn Miyagi production-building expansion tracked in recent issues.

entities.name: Shin-Etsu Chemical
entities.desc: An upstream semiconductor materials monopoly, largely invisible to the AI narrative but critical to it. Shin-Etsu's semiconductor-grade silicon wafers are the substrate on which virtually every chip in this landscape is made. **Market position:** With SUMCO, Shin-Etsu holds a combined ~60% of the global silicon wafer market — a near-duopoly on the most upstream critical semiconductor input. **AI demand impact:** Each new AI training fab (TSMC N2 at Kumamoto, Intel 18A, Samsung SF2) directly increases silicon wafer demand. Shin-Etsu's pricing power in a constrained wafer market gives it structural upside in any AI-driven capex cycle. **Rare-earth magnets:** A significant second business line — permanent magnets are critical for EV motors and humanoid robot actuators, two categories growing at AI-driven pace. **China rare-earth curbs squeeze magnet inputs (#82, Aug 17, 2026):** Japan imported just 13 tons of dysprosium (ジスプロシウム) in 1H26, down 82% YoY, with zero imports recorded in four of the first six months; yttrium imports fell 74% to 204 tons. European dysprosium prices have risen roughly sevenfold since China's April 2025 export controls took effect, and China's overall rare-earth shipments to Japan fell 43.8% YoY as of June even as shipments to the Netherlands (home to ASML) surged 121.4%. Dysprosium is essential to the high-performance permanent magnets Shin-Etsu supplies for EV and hybrid motors, while yttrium coats chipmaking equipment components — meaning the squeeze hits both of Shin-Etsu's core AI-adjacent businesses at once. Japan is diversifying supply (yttrium now sourced from 12 non-China countries in 1H26) and expanding recycling, but alternative volumes remain far short of what's needed to replace China as the dominant supplier. **China imposes anti-dumping deposits up to 99.2% on Japanese DCS (#102, Sept 9, 2026):** China's Commerce Ministry imposed provisional anti-dumping deposits of 80.8–99.2% on dichlorosilane (DCS) imports from Japan effective Sept 8, following a probe opened in January 2026 that found Japanese DCS dumping had caused material injury to domestic producers. Shin-Etsu and Denal Silane are named exporters; Shin-Etsu shares fell 3.4% in Tokyo on the news while Chinese rivals Tangshan Sunfar Silicon and Hubei Heyuan Gas jumped their 10% daily limit. DCS is a specialty gas used in chemical-vapor-deposition steps for logic and memory chips, and Japan is the leading global producer of the ultrapure grade. Shin-Etsu said any revenue impact would not be significant, but the measure — layered on top of the existing rare-earth/dysprosium supply squeeze — adds a second front of China-directed trade friction against a company sitting at the top of the global wafer and specialty-materials supply chain. **Named alongside SUMCO in UBS's wafer-supercycle thesis; renegotiating existing contracts upward (#118, Sept 22, 2026):** UBS kept a Buy rating on Shin-Etsu as part of the same research note arguing 12-inch wafer prices need to rise 40-50% industry-wide to justify new capacity against utilization climbing from 84% (2026) toward 99% (2028). Distinct from SUMCO's public capacity-discipline stance, Shin-Etsu is reported to be actively renegotiating prices under contracts already in force, citing higher electricity, raw-material, and logistics costs -- a live repricing action rather than forward guidance. Shin-Etsu and SUMCO together control more than half of the global wafer market and the strongest share of advanced 300mm epitaxial supply, the segment AI-linked demand needs most; wafers are only 3-5% of total chip manufacturing cost, which limits how much pushback chipmakers can credibly offer.

entities.name: SUMCO
entities.desc: World's #2 silicon wafer maker — a near-duopoly infrastructure position alongside Shin-Etsu Chemical. Silicon wafers are the foundational substrate of every chip in this landscape. **Capacity investment:** SUMCO committed to major new 300mm wafer capacity in Kyushu, co-located with the emerging 'Silicon Island Kyushu' ecosystem (TSMC JASM, Renesas, Sony). **AI capex cycle:** AI chip demand directly increases 300mm silicon wafer demand — each new HBM stack and leading-edge logic chip requires pristine silicon wafer substrates. SUMCO benefits from the structural fab capex boom as a commodity infrastructure play with high barriers to entry (years to build new capacity; exacting quality specs for advanced node wafers). **UBS quantifies the wafer-pricing squeeze SUMCO has been flagging since August (#118, Sept 22, 2026):** UBS raised its global 12-inch wafer demand-growth forecasts (11% for 2026, 14% for 2027, 13% for 2028) and projected industry utilization climbing from 84% in 2026 to 99% by 2028, concluding that avoiding a severe shortage after 2028 requires price increases of 40-50% -- because current operating margins of roughly 12.3% sit well below the 18.3% average manufacturers earned in 2017-2022, leaving little incentive to add capacity. UBS rated SUMCO Neutral with a Y4,000 target, versus Buy on Shin-Etsu Chemical and Siltronic/GlobalWafers. The report puts a number on the same point SUMCO's president made after the company's early-August operating loss despite record 300mm shipment volumes -- that 5-10% price increases "would not have a meaningful impact" -- and reinforces that SUMCO and Shin-Etsu together hold the strongest position in the advanced 300mm epitaxial segment where AI-linked demand and margins concentrate, with wafers only 3-5% of total chip manufacturing cost giving chipmakers little room to resist paying more to secure supply.

entities.name: Ajinomoto
entities.desc: A food and seasonings company that, almost by accident of its amino-acid chemistry business, controls one of the most concentrated chokepoints in the global chip-packaging supply chain. **ABF near-monopoly (#93, Aug 19-31, 2026):** Ajinomoto derived ABF (Ajinomoto Build-up Film) — the insulating build-up film used in nearly every high-end chip package, including the FC-BGA substrates under Nvidia, AMD, and Intel AI accelerators — from its amino-acid chemistry in the 1990s, and now holds over 95% of the global market; China's domestic self-sufficiency sits below 5%. **Reported 30% supply cut to China (Aug 19, 2026):** Chinese outlet JW Insights reported, citing unnamed supply-chain sources, that Ajinomoto has told mainland Chinese customers (Shennan Circuits, Xingsen Technology, Shenghong Electronics) it will cut ABF supply by roughly 30%, prioritizing Japanese and core overseas accounts as production runs at full utilization (~2M sqm/month). The move follows China's January restriction on rare-earth exports to Japan-linked military end users and an 82% YoY drop in Japan's dysprosium imports from China — giving the ABF cut what one report called 'obvious retaliatory optics,' even though every account attributes it to AI-driven capacity allocation rather than policy. **Confirmed price hike, unconfirmed volume cut:** A roughly 30% ABF price increase (notified to substrate makers in May, effective this quarter) is confirmed; the 30% volume cut is not. Ajinomoto has committed ¥25bn since 2023 to expand capacity ~50% by 2030, with a third plant (Kani City, Gifu) not expected online until ~2032 — meaning near-term supply stays structurally tight regardless of the allocation dispute. Goldman Sachs forecasts the global ABF supply-demand gap widening from ~10% in 2H26 to 42% by 2028.

entities.name: Fanuc
entities.desc: **Hitachi physical AI partnership (#127, Sept 30, 2026):** Fanuc and Hitachi signed a strategic partnership pairing Fanuc robots and controllers with Hitachi's HMAX Industry AI and edge AI chips. Trials at Hitachi's Ibaraki plants target parts picking and line changeovers; joint global sales start in FY2027 using both companies' customer bases. entities.name: Bank of Japan (BOJ)
entities.desc: **August real wages up 1.5%, eighth straight gain (#131, Oct 7, 2026):** Labour ministry data showed real wages up 1.5% y/y (consensus 1.5%; July revised 2.0%), the longest run of gains in almost a decade. Nominal pay rose 3.8% to ¥311,364 and base pay 3.8% (unchanged), overtime 5.2%, bonuses flat. The deflator held at 2.2% versus 3.1% a year earlier, as Takaichi-era energy relief and tax cuts held down measured inflation.
