Sakura report Oct 8, household spending Oct 9, national CPI Oct 23. **Uchida ties AI to the neutral rate (#129, Oct 5, 2026):** Deputy Governor Shinichi Uchida, opening the ECONDAT 2026 Fall Meeting, called AI a large positive demand shock lifting activity and prices. AI-driven equity gains have eased financial conditions while heavy bond issuance by AI companies pushes long-term yields up; over time AI could raise productivity and the natural rate of interest, though he said scope and timing are unclear. USD/JPY dipped to about ¥157.5 before returning toward ¥158; the Nikkei briefly topped 70,000 the same day. October hike odds near one in four; MPM Oct 29-30. **Week ahead (#127, Oct 5-9, 2026):** Policy rate 1.25%. The Sept 30 Summary of Opinions showed no rush for October and roughly halved swaps-implied October hike odds before Tokyo core CPI jumped to 2.7%. Ueda addresses the 全国証券大会 (National Securities Convention) Oct 6 at 15:35 JST; August wages Oct 7; Regional Economic Report and branch managers' reports Oct 8; household spending Oct 9. PM Takaichi's Oct 5 policy speech is expected to cap new JGB issuance at ¥40tn and tie issuance to rate moves. USD/JPY near ¥158. MPM Oct 29-30. **Tokyo CPI jumps (#126, Oct 2, 2026):** September Tokyo core CPI (ex fresh food) rose 2.7% y/y from 1.8%, above a 2.4% forecast and the fastest in ten months; headline 2.7% (from 1.9%), core-core 3.0% (from 2.0%), services 2.3% (from 1.4%), helped by the end of water subsidies plus food, transport and hotel price rises. August unemployment rose to 2.5% (2.4% expected); jobs ratio 1.18. USD/JPY steady near ¥158. Revives October hike odds that the Tankan had lowered; national CPI Oct 23, MPM Oct 29-30. **September Tankan (#125, Oct 1, 2026):** Large-manufacturer DI rose 2 to +24, a sixth straight gain but below +25/+26 forecasts; large non-manufacturers fell 2 to +35, first drop in five quarters; small manufacturers +14 vs +11 expected; both large groups see worse conditions by December (mfr +21). Large-firm FY2026 capex +11%, small firms -5%; assumed USD/JPY ¥154.23 vs ~¥157 market; one-year inflation expectation 2.6% (from 2.7%). Read as easing pressure for an October hike after September's move to 1.25%. Japan's central bank. Governor: Kazuo Ueda (植田和男). Policy rate: 0.75% (held April 2026, 6–3 vote split). Raised FY2026 core CPI forecast to 2.8% from 1.9%. OIS pricing June 2026: 77% probability of 25bp hike to 1.00% at June 15–16 MPM. Three dissenters favoured immediate hike. OECD projects 2.0% by end-2027. JGB purchase commitment signal at June MPM is the key 'hawkish rates / dovish duration' watch. **Q2 2026 Tankan (#31, #32, Jul 1 2026):** Large manufacturer DI +22 (vs. +16 consensus; beat by 6 pts; highest since 2018). Non-manufacturer DI +37 (highest since 1991). Capex actual +11.5% FY2026/27. Recurring profits guidance -6.7% (capex-despite-margin-pressure confirms automation bet). BOJ raised policy rate to 1.00% Jun 16; July 30-31 MPM next key date. AI-specific survey items added in 2026 Tankan — first explicit capex monitoring for AI infrastructure. **JGB yield milestones (#33, #35, Jul 2026):** 10-year JGB new-issue coupon set at 2.7% (29-year high) in Jul 2 MoF auction. Yield then hit 2.81% on Jul 3 (30-year high) on fiscal concerns under PM Takaichi. By mid-July trading near 2.9% (30-year-plus high). Nikkei whipsawed 2,100 points intraday Jul 3; higher JGB yields simultaneously tighten financial conditions and validate the rate-normalization thesis supporting financials. **June PPI 7.1% (#42):** Corporate goods prices +7.1% YoY in June — keeps BOJ rate-hike bets pointed at October even as July 30-31 MPM expected to hold at 1.00%. **MUFG milestone (#45, Jul 13 2026):** Mitsubishi UFJ Financial Group overtook Toyota as Japan's most valuable listed company by market cap — first bank to top the league table in a generation. Proximate driver: BOJ at 1.00% (three-decade high) + 10-year JGB near 2.9% (30-year high) reprices bank deposit franchises as earning assets. BOJ July 30-31 Outlook Report: sources indicate likely FY2026 growth upgrade with hold at 1.00%. **Meeting opens amid yen/bond stress (#60, Jul 30 2026):** The two-day policy meeting opens today with consensus still pointing to a hold at 1.00% and an FY2026 growth-forecast upgrade (toward ~0.8%, up from April's 0.5%), supported by resilient AI/semiconductor demand. The decision, due July 31 with Ueda's 3:30pm JST press conference, lands against a weaker yen (near ¥163.7) and a 40-year JGB yield close to its May record — meaning the market-relevant question is less the hold itself than whether Ueda's language leans hawkish enough to validate an autumn hike. **Decision day: hold at 1.00%, GDP forecast upgraded (#61, Jul 31, 2026):** The BOJ held its policy rate at 1.00% as universally expected (52/52 Bloomberg-surveyed economists), closing the two-day meeting that opened Jul 30. The quarterly Outlook Report upgraded the FY2026 real GDP forecast to 0.8% (from April's 0.5%), citing resilient AI/semiconductor-linked capex. With the hold itself priced in, the market-moving variable was Ueda's afternoon press conference — specifically whether his language signals an autumn rate hike is coming sooner than consensus assumes, against a yen near a 40-year low and JGB yields near their May record. **Outlook Report full text + inflation trajectory (#66, Aug 3, 2026):** The full-text Outlook for Economic Activity and Prices (July 2026), released two business days after the Jul 31 decision, sets the FY2026 core CPI trajectory to accelerate to a level 'clearly above 2%' from H2 FY2026, with medium-to-long-term inflation expectations converging near 2% through FY2027. The Board explicitly frames risks to prices as skewed to the upside — driven by persistent yen weakness, robust global AI-linked demand for chips and electronic equipment feeding through to consumer goods, and elevated logistics costs from Middle East shipping disruption — a notably more hawkish risk framing than the growth-upgrade headline alone suggested. Next checkpoints: July CPI (Aug 21) and August CPI (Sep 18), the core reference data for the September and October policy meetings. **Real wages: sixth straight monthly gain (#67, Aug 4-5, 2026):** June labor-ministry data showed nominal wages up 3.4% YoY — a fifth consecutive month above 3%, the longest such streak in 34 years — while real wages rose 1.7%, a sixth straight month of gains and the longest run since 2021. Base pay (scheduled cash earnings, stripping out bonuses/overtime) rose 2.9% for full-time workers. Governor Ueda has flagged upside price risks as grounds for a hike 'as soon as September'; the wage data reinforces the case for sustained income growth underpinning the BOJ's confidence in durable 2% inflation, with July CPI (Aug 21) and August CPI (Sep 18) the next hard checkpoints before the September and October meetings. **IMF backs continued normalization (#69, Aug 6 2026):** IMF First Deputy Managing Director Dan Katz told Bloomberg Television that Japan's economy is undergoing a 'very important long-term transformation' from Abe-era structural reforms now bearing fruit, giving the BOJ room to keep exiting its near three-decade ultra-loose policy regime: 'Inflation is still modestly above target, so I would expect a continued normalization.' The remarks followed the first joint US-Japan yen intervention in 15 years; Bank of America revised its year-end USD/JPY forecast to 149 (from 152) and said a September rather than October hike would let the BOJ 'demonstrate its resolve' on upside inflation risk. Yen traded near ¥158.2 as of Aug 6, down ~1.3% from its Aug 3 high. External validation of the domestic case (Aug 4-5 wage data, Aug 3 Outlook Report) for a September move. **Summary of Opinions: Jul 31 meeting, hawkish tilt on timing (#71, Aug 10, 2026):** The Summary of Opinions from the Jul 30-31 meeting — where the Board held the policy rate at 1.00% by an 8-1 vote, Hajime Takata dissenting in favor of an immediate hike to 1.25% — was published Aug 10. Several members judged economic activity and prices are developing in line with the Bank's outlook; some argued there is room to raise a policy rate that remains 'significantly low' given negative real interest rates near 25-year lows, while others said more data was needed before moving. One opinion explicitly framed timely hikes as a way to avoid being forced into rapid, economically damaging tightening later, and members continue to eye a neutral rate of 'at least around 1%' as the medium-term reference point. The published opinions stop short of naming a date, but combined with Ueda's public 'as soon as September' framing, the Aug 3 Outlook Report's upside-skewed inflation risk language, and the Aug 4-5 real-wage data, market consensus continues to coalesce around September or October as the next live meeting. Next hard checkpoints: July CPI (Aug 21) and August CPI (Sep 18). **July PPI eases but stays elevated (#75, Aug 13, 2026):** Producer prices rose 7.2% YoY in July, undershooting the 7.4% Reuters-polled consensus and down from a revised 7.3% in June, with electricity the single largest contributor (+0.23pp) as energy import costs remain elevated following the Iran war and a still-weak yen. The PPI/CPI gap remains unusually wide — headline CPI just 1.9% and core 1.6-2.0% — which CNBC and other outlets attribute largely to the Takaichi cabinet's energy subsidies shielding consumers from the full pass-through of wholesale costs. The data reinforces rather than resolves the case for a hike: elevated pipeline inflation keeps a September move alive per Reuters sourcing, but the subsidy-suppressed CPI print gives the Board room to wait for the Aug 21 and Sep 18 CPI checkpoints before committing to a date. **JGB curve reprices on oil-driven inflation risk, Sept hike odds rise to 78% (Aug 12, 2026):** The 10-year JGB yield rose 4.5bp to 2.850%, the 5-year yield rose 2.5bp to a record 2.110%, and the 2-year yield — most sensitive to BOJ policy — rose 3.5bp to 1.645%, the highest since May 1995, as Brent crude gained on renewed Strait of Hormuz risk after Iran's top security official said the shipping route stays closed absent a US concession. Tokyo Tanshi data showed markets pricing a 78% probability of a September hike, up from 66% the prior session, reinforced by the hawkish tone of the BOJ's Jul 31 Summary of Opinions (published Aug 10). The 20-year yield rose 3bp to 3.715% and the 30-year rose 4bp to 3.990% — the entire curve, not just the short end, repricing for both earlier BOJ tightening and imported energy inflation. **Q2 GDP release day (Aug 17, 2026):** The Cabinet Office's preliminary April-June GDP print — the last major data checkpoint before the Sept 17-18 MPM alongside the Aug 21 and Sep 18 CPI reports — was due today; the average forecast of 10 private-sector think tanks pointed to a third straight quarterly expansion of around +2.1% annualized (+0.5% q/q), led by private consumption (real-wage gains, easing food inflation) and a modest export drag from softer Middle East-bound shipments. A print at or above consensus would reinforce the Board's 'as soon as September' framing; a miss would hand the wait-for-more-data camp fresh ammunition. **Q2 GDP miss, but Sept hike odds hold near 80% (Aug 17-18, 2026):** The Cabinet Office's preliminary April-June GDP print undershot consensus at +0.3% q/q (+1.1% annualized) versus the ~+2.1% annualized private-sector forecast, dragged down by softer capex and private consumption. Despite the miss, overnight swaps continued to imply roughly an 80% probability of a September 18 hike, with long-term JGB yields hitting a fresh three-decade high as investors read the soft print as reflecting one-off factors rather than a change in the underlying inflation trajectory — the GDP deflator rose 2.6% YoY, keeping price pressure the dominant signal over the growth wobble. The setup leaves the Board balancing a softer domestic-demand picture against sticky inflation, with the Aug 21 and Sep 18 CPI prints as the next hard checkpoints before the Sept 17-18 meeting. **Nikkei's sharpest drop of the run as Hormuz risk resurfaces (#81, Aug 18 2026):** The Nikkei 225 fell 1.6% to 68,098.54, snapping a five-session, 5.5% winning streak, after the US-Iran ceasefire lapsed — Washington ruled out an extension and Tehran signaled a shift to a 'fully offensive' posture — and Strait of Hormuz shipping again ground to a halt. Crude's jump revived global inflation concern and pushed the 10-year JGB yield to a fresh three-decade high near 2.95%, with chip-linked names (Tokyo Electron -2.9%, Advantest -1.7%, Lasertec -1.6%) leading the decline as higher rates compressed already-elevated AI-rally valuations. The episode is a reminder that Japan's twin 2026 narratives — a chip-led equity rally and a slow-motion BOJ normalization — share a single vulnerability: an external energy-price shock that raises both inflation expectations (pulling the BOJ hawkish) and the discount rate applied to richly-valued growth stocks at the same time. **Mizuho markets head: hike 'as soon as next month,' possibly more frequent (#83, Aug 18, 2026):** Kenya Koshimizu, co-head of Mizuho's global markets division (which manages the bank's ¥41T/$257B securities portfolio), told Bloomberg he expects the BOJ to move as soon as September and potentially adopt a faster hiking cadence than the market has priced, citing persistent yen weakness and inflation running above target. He also flagged that longer-dated JGB yields should keep climbing after the 10-year hit a fresh 30-year high the same week. The comments landed alongside continued bond-market repricing — Bloomberg reported Japan's bond yields climbing on BOJ hike bets and fiscal concerns on Aug 17 — and were followed by a broad-based Nikkei 225 rally to 66,118 (+1.21%) on Aug 20 as global bond yields pulled back after the US Treasury expanded its buyback program, temporarily easing the same rate anxiety driving the BOJ-hike narrative. **Weak yen sharpens the hike case; commentary turns explicitly critical of delay (#84, Aug 21, 2026):** Bloomberg reported that persistent yen weakness is prompting louder calls — from sell-side desks and commentators alike — for the BOJ to move faster, framing September 18 as the live meeting with roughly a 74% probability priced by swaps markets, alongside an October alternative. Forbes contributor William Pesek characterized the BOJ's position as an increasingly acute 'rate-hike dilemma': every month of delay lets yen weakness feed import-price inflation further, but a hike into softer Q2 GDP data (+0.3% q/q) and elevated JGB yields already near three-decade highs risks compounding financial-stability stress the Board would rather avoid. The through-line from Aug 17-20 coverage holds: inflation risk (via a weak yen and Hormuz-driven energy costs) continues to outweigh the growth wobble in the Board's reaction function, keeping September the base case while leaving execution risk (JGB market absorption, bank balance-sheet effects) as the second-order variable analysts are now debating in place of the hike/no-hike question itself. **July CPI resolves the checkpoint hawkish; three-speech telegraph begins (#87, Aug 21-23, 2026):** July core CPI (ex-fresh food) rose 1.8% YoY, accelerating from June's 1.6% and beating the checkpoint the Board had flagged as the next hard data point; core-core (ex-fresh food and energy) rose 1.9%. Swaps pricing moved to roughly 82% for a September 18 hike to 1.25%, and Bloomberg reported the BOJ has lined up three board-member speeches ahead of the Sept 17-18 meeting — Deputy Governor Ryozo Himino's Aug 27 address to Saitama business leaders is the first, mirroring the pre-hike telegraphing pattern the Bank used before its 2024 and June 2026 moves. USD/JPY traded near ¥159, with the weak yen itself now cited as reinforcing rather than merely coinciding with the inflation case. **Himino kicks off the three-speech telegraph (#89, Aug 27, 2026):** Deputy Governor Ryozo Himino delivered the first of three pre-MPM board speeches, addressing business leaders in Saitama; his remarks were the most closely watched of the three because of his track record as a hawkish-leaning voice and because markets read the tone he sets as a template for board member Hajime Takata (speaking Sept 2) and Kazuyuki Masu (Sept 10). The sequence sits alongside a G20 finance leaders' meeting (Aug 31–Sep 1) where Governor Ueda may meet US Treasury Secretary Scott Bessent, whose past comments on Japanese policy have preceded BOJ hikes; Nomura's Mari Iwashita flagged that pattern as one more reason the swaps market has settled near an 80%+ probability of a September 18 move. The three-speech, one-summit run-up leaves the Sept 17-18 meeting with unusually dense pre-positioning relative to prior cycles. **July data complicates the setup: record-low unemployment vs. weak output and spending (#93, Aug 29, 2026):** July's data cluster gave the Board a genuinely split picture. The unemployment rate fell to a post-pandemic low of 2.3% (vs. 2.5% consensus), with the job-to-applicant ratio holding at 1.22 — the tight-labor-market leg of the hike case. But industrial production fell 1.6% m/m (vs. -1.1% expected), dragged by car output (-7.6%) and semiconductor-manufacturing-equipment output (-16.4%), and retail sales fell 1.6% (vs. -0.2% expected), broadly based. The mix — tight labor market, soft output and consumption — is the same tension the Board has been navigating since the Q2 GDP miss (Aug 17-18): sticky, import-driven inflation continues to outweigh growth wobbles in the reaction function, keeping September the base case, but it adds a fresh data point for the wait-for-more-information camp ahead of the Sept 17-18 meeting. **10-year JGB yield crosses 3% for the first time since 1996; Takata speaks Sept 2 (#95, Sept 1-2, 2026):** The 10-year JGB yield pushed through 3% intraday on Sept 1 — a level last seen in 1996 — as a second consecutive session of Middle East-linked oil gains compounded the same inflation-and-fiscal-concern repricing that has driven the curve higher since Aug 12. The yen slipped to ¥160.08, giving up most of the ground won in the late-July US-Japan joint intervention, with swaps pricing roughly 73% odds of a September 18 hike — little changed from late August, suggesting the move is now substantially priced rather than a fresh catalyst. Board member Hajime Takata delivers the second of the three pre-MPM telegraph speeches on Sept 2, addressing business leaders with markets watching for confirmation of the hawkish framing Himino set on Aug 27; Kazuyuki Masu's Sept 10 address remains the final data point before the Sept 17-18 meeting. Chip-linked equities (Tokyo Electron -3.4%, Advantest -1.6%) led the Nikkei 225 (-0.15% to 66,215) lower on the same yield move, even as the broader Topix rose 0.62% — a reminder that higher discount rates now hit AI-capex-linked growth names disproportionately even when the index itself holds up. **Ueda hints at September hike from G20, sidesteps daily market comment (#96, Sept 2, 2026):** Speaking to reporters after a G20 finance ministers and central bankers meeting in Asheville, North Carolina, Governor Ueda said the Board will hold a 'thorough debate' on policy at every meeting including Sept 17-18, and flagged upside price risks — Middle East-linked energy costs, resilient AI-related demand, and weak-yen import inflation — as the factors the Board will weigh. He declined to comment on day-to-day JGB or yen moves, including the Sept 1 break above 3% on the 10-year, but did not push back on market pricing (~73-78% odds) of a September move. Combined with Takata's Sept 2 Saitama-adjacent telegraph speech, this is the clearest on-the-record signal yet from the Governor himself, rather than deputies or swaps pricing, that a hike is the base case rather than a tail risk. **Carry-trade unwind sends yen to one-month high; intervention chatter returns (#98, Sept 3-4, 2026):** The yen jumped over 2% against the dollar, touching ¥155.28, as traders unwound yen-funded carry trades in response to hawkish Ueda and Takata commentary raising the prospect of a larger-than-usual hike at the Sept 17-18 meeting — the sharpest single move of the pre-meeting run-up and a shift from the gradual, speech-by-speech repricing seen through August. The move puts Ministry of Finance intervention chatter back on trading desks for the first time since the joint US-Japan intervention in late July, and adds a new risk axis heading into the meeting: not just whether the Board hikes, but how disorderly the yen move is if it does. US nonfarm payrolls (Sept 5) is the next data point that could reset relative Fed-BOJ rate expectations before the MPM. **Cabinet Office BCI: fourth straight 'Improving' reading, AI-chip equipment cited as the driver (#101, Sept 7, 2026):** The preliminary July 2026 Business Conditions Index kept its 'Improving' assessment for a fourth consecutive month, the longest such streak in years — coincident index at 120.1 (+1.6pt m/m), leading index +1.7pt. Tech Times attributed the reading largely to AI-driven semiconductor-equipment orders flowing through Tokyo Electron and peers (Shin-Etsu, Lasertec), citing SEMI's record $36.55bn Q1 2026 global equipment billings (+14% YoY) and a Semiconductor Equipment Association of Japan forecast of >¥5tn in FY2026 Japan-made tool sales, a first. JPMorgan's Ayako Fujita said a September hike delay 'would likely shake market stability' given how priced-in the move now is. The report also surfaced a genuine tension the Board must weigh: Q2 2026 GDP (Aug 17 release) showed domestic demand -0.2% q/q, business equipment investment -1.2%, and private consumption -0.1%, with growth driven almost entirely by external, AI-linked export demand — meaning four straight 'Improving' BCI prints reflect a structurally narrow, equipment-sector-led recovery rather than a broad-based one, a distinction the Board will have to account for in its Sept 17-18 decision on a hike to 1.25%. **Bessent jawbones the yen higher; Takata raises an outsized-hike prospect; Reuters Tankan confirms AI-capex strength (#103, Sept 9-10, 2026):** US Treasury Secretary Scott Bessent's public commentary pushing for yen strength helped drive the currency toward ¥153/dollar this week -- its strongest level since February, up more than 2% the prior week -- with markets now pricing a BOJ tightening path more aggressive than the Bank may actually deliver at the confirmed September 18 meeting. Board member Hajime Takata (whose Sept 2 telegraph speech was flagged above) raised the explicit possibility of an outsized or back-to-back additional hike rather than a standard 25bp move, while Ueda reiterated the Board needs to watch upside price risks closely. Independently, the September Reuters Tankan poll (fielded Aug 26-Sept 4, published Sept 9) showed the manufacturer sentiment index climbing to +21 from +18 in August -- the highest since December 2021 -- with the electronics sub-index surging to +39 from +24, driven by AI-linked semiconductor and data-center demand; non-manufacturer sentiment held steady at +29. The setup is asymmetric: political jawboning and a strong private survey both point toward a hawkish outcome, but if the Board delivers only the widely-expected quarter-point instead of Takata's outsized alternative, the yen's Bessent-driven gains could reverse quickly once the meeting resolves the gap between priced-in expectations and what the BOJ actually decides. **Yen strength since the late-July intervention breaks manufacturers' FY forecasts (#106, Sept 12, 2026):** Nikkei reported (via QUICK data) that of 360 major Japanese companies disclosing FY2026 (ending March 2027) exchange-rate assumptions, 150 built plans on ¥155-159/dollar and 35 on ¥160-164, while the yen has since strengthened to roughly ¥153-154 -- below every one of those assumption bands. Toyota estimates each ¥1 gain cuts annual consolidated operating profit by about ¥50 billion; Daiwa Securities' Kenji Abe calculated a ¥1 gain cuts aggregate pretax profit at Japan's listed companies by roughly 0.3%. The yen has gained about ¥10 against the dollar since the joint US-Japan intervention in late July, reversing the weak-yen tailwind that had been inflating overseas-subsidiary profits and export margins -- a structural earnings risk distinct from the jawboning/hike-timing question tracked above, and one that compounds if the Sept 17-18 meeting delivers a larger-than-expected hike. **August PPI stays elevated, reinforcing the case for a Sept 17-18 hike (#107, Sept 14, 2026):** Japan's producer price index rose 7.6% y/y in August, ahead of the 7.4% consensus and following an upwardly revised 7.7% July gain; the advance was led by oil and coal products, chemical products, ICT equipment, and nonferrous metals, with companies continuing to pass through elevated energy, shipping, packaging, and wage costs. The month-on-month print eased 0.2% after a 0.4% July rise, but the year-on-year rate remains close to a three-and-a-half-year high. Reuters' post-release poll showed all 52 surveyed BOJ watchers expecting the Sept 17-18 meeting to raise the policy rate to 1.25%, with a majority now pencilling in a follow-up move to 1.75% as soon as Q2 2027 -- earlier than previously assumed. The PPI print is a distinct data input from the yen-weakness and JGB-auction threads tracked in recent issues: it is a cost-push inflation signal on the demand side of the hike case, reinforcing rather than duplicating the currency and bond-market pressure already pushing Ueda toward a move next week. **Decision day arrives with consensus near-unanimous (#111, Sept 17-18, 2026):** The two-day meeting concludes today with a Reuters poll (fielded Sept 1-8) showing 66 of 68 economists (97%) expecting a 25bp hike to 1.25% -- up sharply from 57% in the prior survey -- which would be the highest policy rate since 1993 and mark the fastest hiking pace since the early 1990s. 62% of respondents now see the rate reaching at least 1.75% by end-Q2 2027, three months earlier than August's poll implied, while half of those who answered an extra question still pick 1.75% as the terminal rate, though the share favoring 2.00%-or-higher has risen to 40% from 23% in July. With the hike itself fully priced, the tradeable content sits almost entirely in Ueda's 3:30pm JST press conference: whether his language endorses the faster-than-expected path markets have now built in, or pushes back toward the more gradual cadence the Board signaled as recently as July. **Hike delivered: 25bp to 1.25%, 7-2 split vote, Ueda won't rule out 50bp move (#112, Sept 18, 2026):** The Board raised the policy rate 25bp to 1.25% -- the highest since 1995 -- resolving the near-unanimous consensus (66/68 economists) built up over the prior two weeks of telegraphing. The vote split 7-2, with reflationist dissenters Toichiro Asada and Ayano Sato (both appointed by PM Takaichi earlier in 2026) voting to hold, arguing core inflation below 2% doesn't yet justify tightening. The yen fell on the dissent count -- two holdouts read as a softer signal on the pace of further hikes than the pre-meeting unanimous-consensus framing implied. At the 3:30pm press conference, Governor Ueda said underlying inflation is 'quite close to 2 percent' and explicitly declined to rule out a 50bp increment at a future meeting, keeping the faster-cadence scenario (Takata's Sept 9-10 remarks, the 62% of economists pricing 1.75% by Q2 2027) alive despite the two dissents. Next checkpoints: October MPM and the Q3 Tankan. **Fed and BOJ both hike same week; Nikkei/TOPIX sell off into holiday close (#115, Sept 16-21, 2026):** The Fed raised its target range 25bp to 3.75%-4.00% on Sept 16 -- its first hike since 2023, a 12-0 vote citing 'inflation remains elevated' -- two days before the BOJ's own 25bp move to 1.25%. The rare same-week convergence of Fed and BOJ tightening pressured Japanese equities: the Nikkei 225 fell 1.55% and the broader TOPIX 1.83% over the week, led by exporters and high-multiple growth names most exposed to a firmer yen and higher discount rates. Markets then sat out Sept 21 for Keiro no Hi (敬老の日, Respect for the Aged Day), leaving the reopening session as the first read on whether the double-hike selloff extends or stabilizes. **Sept 18 hike fails to stabilize yen as markets reopen (#117, Sept 24, 2026):** The 7-2 dissenting vote on the Sept 18 hike to 1.25% (highest since 1995) is being read by traders as a signal that further tightening will be harder to deliver, which is why the yen kept weakening into the Sept 21-23 Silver Week closure rather than firming on the rate move. Nikkei futures traded during the holiday were pricing about 2.5% above the Sept 18 cash close of 65,018.95, pointing to a firmer reopen on Sept 24 driven by a global AI-linked rally rather than by domestic monetary policy. **Q3 Tankan preview (#121, due Oct 1, 2026):** Average of 12 private forecasters sees large manufacturers' DI at +26 (up 4, sixth straight gain on AI/chip demand) and large non-manufacturers at +36 (down 1 on weak inbound tourism and costs). Bloomberg reported underlying price-trend gauges quickened in August. US backing for a stronger yen (Sept 25) gives political cover for a further hike at the late-October MPM. **Output miss before the September Tankan (#124, Sept 30-Oct 1, 2026):** August industrial production fell 1.7% m/m against a forecast 1.7% rise, the second straight drop, led by a 6.8% fall in motor vehicles; retail sales rose 2.7% y/y vs about 3.3-3.5% expected. Manufacturers project +3.2% in September and +3.1% in October. September Tankan due Oct 1 at 8:50 JST with think-tank consensus for large manufacturers at +26 (June +22). Policy rate 1.25% after the September hike; a former BOJ executive puts October hike odds at 20-30%.

entities.desc: **August current account: ¥4.06tn surplus on record primary income (#132, Oct 8, 2026):** MoF's preliminary balance of payments showed a ¥4.062tn surplus, well above the ¥3.19tn consensus and the 19th straight monthly surplus. Primary income hit a record ¥5.133tn (+21.6% y/y, highest since 1985 records), while the goods balance swung to a ¥687.7bn deficit and services posted a ¥115.8bn deficit. A weaker yen (down about 7.5% against the dollar y/y) inflated the yen value of overseas returns. **10-year auction draws strongest demand since May (#130, Oct 6, 2026):** The new 10-year JGB carried a 3.1% coupon (up from 2.7%); bid-to-cover was 3.76 versus 3.29 in September and a 12-month average of 3.21, and the tail narrowed to 0.02 from 0.12. The 10-year yield touched 3.115%, matching its highest since 1996, while the 20-year hit 3.99% and the 30-year held near its 4.235% record. A day earlier Takaichi told the Diet she would 'control' bond issuance. The 30-year auction follows on Oct 8. Japan's fiscal authority. Finance Minister: Satsuki Katayama (片山さつき). Authorized record ¥11.73T (~$74B) FX intervention (為替介入) April 28–May 27, 2026 — first since July 2024, surpassing prior monthly record. USD/JPY hit ¥155 then retraced to 159.3. Issued fresh verbal warnings June 2026. 300bp US-Japan rate gap drives structural yen carry trade pressure. **JGB new-issue coupon 2.7% (#33, Jul 2 2026):** MoF's auction of new 10-year JGB set coupon at 2.7% — highest new-issue coupon in 29 years. Auction described as soft (subscription ratio below prior levels), signaling JGB supply/demand tension as Takaichi's fiscal stance raises long-end vigilance. **Ambush FX intervention (#34, Jul 3–4 2026):** USD/JPY hit four-decade low near 162.8; roughly 1% yen surge occurred in holiday-thinned July 3–4 US trading — consistent with MoF's unannounced 'ambush' intervention tactics (not officially confirmed; MOF has declined to comment). Yen near 1986 lows entering Q3 2026. **Goldman 165 call (#38, Jul 8 2026):** Goldman Sachs cut 12-month USD/JPY forecast to 165 — among Wall Street's most bearish. Thesis: structural carry-trade pressure and US-Japan rate differential keep yen weak despite intervention risk. **GPIF head-fake (#41, Jul 11 2026):** Finance Minister Katayama said government will explore measures encouraging Japan's pension funds to substantially increase domestic asset holdings. Response was immediate: yen firmed toward 161, 10-year JGB yield pulled back from 30-year highs, Nikkei rose 1.2%. Described as a positioning squeeze (kuchisaki kainyū — verbal intervention) — GPIF formal allocation changes move through review processes, not press conferences. Concrete follow-up required to validate. **Intervention rally fades, current account surprise deficit (#72, Aug 10 2026):** The yen weakened as much as 1% to ¥159.35/$ on Aug 10 — the worst performer among G-10 currencies that day — erasing roughly half the gain from the Jul 31 US-Japan joint intervention (itself the first such coordinated action since 2011). MoF data released the same day showed Japan's current account unexpectedly swung to a ¥92.3bn deficit in June, adding a fundamentals-based headwind on top of the structural US-Japan rate differential. Katayama has repeated that authorities 'will not hesitate' to intervene again and disclosed plans to draw on the Fed's FIMA Repo Facility to extend intervention firepower without depleting FX reserves outright — a signal aimed at dispelling doubts about Japan's capacity for repeat action rather than a commitment to a specific defense level. **Intervention gains erode further, yen nears ¥160 (#73, Aug 11, 2026):** The yen weakened toward ¥159.4/$ on Aug 11 — Bloomberg reported it edging toward the 160 line for the first time since the Jul 31 joint US-Japan intervention — as traders test whether authorities will step in a third time. The Japan Times described the move as erasing roughly half of the intervention-driven bounce, compounding the Aug 10 current-account deficit surprise. With ¥160 historically treated as a psychological trigger level and Katayama's FIMA Repo Facility framing intended to signal firepower rather than commit to a specific defense line, the episode keeps intervention credibility — not the hold/hike decision itself — as the market's central near-term question heading into July CPI (Aug 21). **July trade data: exports fastest since Oct 2022, semiconductor equipment +49.1% (#83, Aug 20, 2026):** MoF's trade statistics showed exports up 23.2% YoY in July to ¥11.5T — beating the 19.9% consensus and the fastest pace since October 2022 — powered by a 49.1% jump in semiconductor-equipment shipment value tied to the global AI capex boom, alongside a weak yen (near 40-year lows against the dollar) that inflates yen-denominated export values. The composition matters: export volumes rose just 5.2%, meaning most of the headline gain reflects currency depreciation and higher selling prices rather than genuinely stronger shipment quantities — a reminder that a weak yen is flattering nominal trade figures even as the underlying real-demand picture is more modest. Imports rose faster still, +27.8% to a fresh record ¥12.1T, with petroleum imports up 87.8% on Hormuz-driven oil prices, widening the trade deficit to ¥634.5bn (a third consecutive monthly deficit, though narrower than the ¥680bn expected). Exports to China rose 25.8%, to the US 22%, to the EU 19.1% — broad-based, chip-and-auto-led strength across all three major markets. The data lands as one more upside-inflation data point (via import costs) reinforcing the BOJ's September rate-hike case, even as it flatters Japan's nominal trade headline. **JGB auctions become a global rates story, not just a domestic one (#91, Aug 24-27, 2026):** MoF's Aug 20 20-year JGB auction drew firmer-than-average demand even as the 20-year yield traded near its highest since 1996, and attention has now turned to two auctions in the coming week — 10-year notes on Sept 1 and 30-year bonds on Sept 3 — that Bloomberg and other outlets flagged as a potential trigger for renewed pressure on US Treasury yields. The mechanism: foreign investors now account for roughly 65% of monthly cash trading volume in Japan's government bond market (versus just 12% in 2009), so weak demand at a JGB auction reads as a global, not purely domestic, risk-appetite signal; conversely, rising JGB yields give Japan's own institutions — still holding over $1.1tn in US Treasuries — more reason to keep capital home rather than recycle it into US debt, a structural headwind for Treasury demand independent of Fed policy. With the 10-year JGB yield already near a three-decade high around 2.88-2.9% on BOJ hike expectations, the Sept 1 and Sept 3 auctions are shaping up as an early test of whether fiscal-concern-driven JGB weakness (Takaichi-era spending plans, a shrinking pool of domestic buyers) can now transmit directly into US long-end pricing — a channel institutional investors have historically discounted but which foreign-ownership concentration has made structurally more plausible in 2026. **Yen breaks ¥160, erasing more than half the July intervention gain (#92, Aug 28-29, 2026):** USD/JPY weakened past ¥160 for the first time since the Jul 31 joint US-Japan intervention, slipping as much as 0.5% to around ¥160.16 after incoming Fed Chair Kevin Warsh vowed to keep hitting the Fed's inflation target — a hawkish-on-inflation, dollar-supportive signal that widened the US-Japan rate differential further. ¥160 is the level markets and Tokyo officials have treated as the psychological/political intervention trigger since the Jul 31 action pushed the pair from ¥160 to ¥155; the retracement means the joint intervention has now given back more than half its gain in under a month. Katayama has not signaled a fresh intervention as of this writing, keeping the same open question live since Aug 10-11: whether authorities view a third action as necessary before the Sept 17-18 BOJ meeting, or whether they let a hawkish September hike do the work of supporting the currency instead. **Record ¥15.39tn confirmed spent on July-August intervention (#93, Aug 28-29, 2026):** MoF disclosed that Japan spent ¥15.39tn (~$96bn) on yen-buying, dollar-selling intervention between July 30 and Aug 26 — the largest monthly total on record, confirming the scale behind the Jul 31 joint US-Japan action. The disclosure lands the same week USD/JPY breached ¥160 again, retracing more than half that intervention's gain; 2026's cumulative intervention total now exceeds ¥27tn, already surpassing the prior full-year record of roughly ¥15tn set in 2024. The confirmed figure gives markets a hard number behind Katayama's repeated 'will not hesitate' rhetoric, but the fact that ¥15.39tn of firepower bought less than a month of yen support before ¥160 gave way again is itself the more market-relevant signal — reinforcing the view among some desks that rate policy, not intervention scale, will have to do more of the work from here. **G20 finance meeting: Bessent tells Japan to hike and end big stimulus (#99, Aug 31, 2026):** At the G20 finance ministers' meeting in Asheville, NC, US Treasury Secretary Scott Bessent told Japan it should accelerate BOJ rate hikes and abandon 'outdated ideas about big economic stimulus' — remarks read domestically as a direct challenge to PM Sanae Takaichi's expansionary fiscal approach, with Bessent reportedly suggesting Japan should instead 'sit back and enjoy the success of Abenomics and let that run.' Bessent separately told Reuters recent yen moves were 'not disorderly,' signaling little US appetite for a third joint intervention despite the record ¥15.39tn already spent in July-August — effectively pushing the policy burden back onto the BOJ's Sept 17-18 hike decision rather than further FX intervention. Japanese officials characterized the comments as Washington escalating its demands on Japanese fiscal and monetary policy simultaneously, adding a US-pressure dimension to the domestic hike debate ahead of the meeting. **Five-year JGB auction draws weakest demand in months (#102, Sept 9, 2026):** MoF's Sept 8 sale of five-year JGBs saw bid-to-cover fall to 3.42 (vs. 4.15 at the prior auction and a 3.44 12-month average) with a wider tail of 0.04 (vs. 0.02 prior) — the softest demand signal in months as investors turn cautious just over a week before the BOJ's Sept 17-18 meeting. The soft auction lands against persistent fiscal-supply concern under PM Takaichi's expansionary agenda: elevated government spending keeps JGB issuance high even as the pool of steady domestic buyers has structurally shrunk, the same dynamic flagged in the Aug 24-27 note on JGB auctions becoming a global, not just domestic, rates story. Separately, Takaichi economic adviser Takuji Aida — a reflationist historically skeptical of BOJ hikes — said he now expects a September hike followed by another by January, pulling forward his own prior forecast of a January 2027 move and adding to a sense of broadening consensus, even among fiscal doves, that further tightening is coming. **Cabinet reshuffle keeps Katayama, unfunded consumption-tax cut heads to parliament (#114, Sept 16-17, 2026):** PM Takaichi's first cabinet reshuffle retained Finance Minister Satsuki Katayama and Economic Revitalization Minister Minoru Kiuchi, signaling continuity for the expansionary spending agenda already pressuring JGB issuance and auction demand in recent issues. The Cabinet adopted a two-year cut in the consumption tax on food from 8% to 1% plus household payouts, but without specifying financing — Takaichi has ruled out deficit-financing bonds while declining to detail an alternative funding path, a gap opposition lawmakers are expected to press when the Diet reconvenes in October. The reshuffle itself left markets largely unmoved (Nikkei flat, yen marginally firmer near ¥155.6, 10-year JGB slightly stronger), but an unfunded tax cut layered on top of already-strained fiscal metrics is a distinct medium-term risk to the same JGB-auction-demand and foreign-investor-share dynamics tracked above, independent of the BOJ's parallel rate-hike path. **August trade data: exports +19.3%, electronic components +52.3%, deficit widens to ¥1.1056tn (#116, Sept 16, 2026):** MoF's August trade statistics showed exports up 19.3% YoY to ¥10.05tn (beating the 18.4% consensus), the 12th consecutive month of export growth, led by a 52.3% surge in electronic-components shipments (including semiconductors) to ¥894.1bn — by far the fastest-growing major export line and a direct readout of the global AI capex cycle already lifting Tokyo Electron's and Kioxia's order books. Imports rose faster still, +28.0% to ¥11.15tn, pushing the trade balance to a ¥1.1056tn ($7.1bn) deficit — the fourth consecutive monthly deficit and the largest since January. The composition split is the read for positioning: semiconductor-linked export strength is a structural, AI-capex story that stands apart from the currency- and energy-driven deficit, and one shouldn't be read as a proxy for the other. **Markets reopen into live intervention watch (#117, Sept 24, 2026):** Tokyo's cash equity market reopened Sept 24 after a five-day Silver Week closure with the yen near ¥157-158/$, its softest level in months, and traders reporting authorities have already run rate checks -- a step that typically precedes intervention. The setup is unusual: the BOJ's Sept 18 rate hike to 1.25% would normally be currency-supportive, but a 7-2 dissenting vote left traders reading limited room for further hikes, so the yen kept weakening instead of stabilizing. That shifts the defense burden back onto MoF intervention, which cost a record ¥15.4tn in a single month earlier in 2026 for only a temporary effect. **Funding gap persists, 10Y JGB yield climbs toward 3%, Oct 5 extraordinary Diet convenes (#119, Sept 17-23, 2026):** The ¥5tn ($32bn)-a-year food consumption-tax cut approved in August still has no identified funding source; Finance Minister Katayama has pushed the decision to the FY2027 budget process due by late December. Of roughly 120 special tax measures expiring in FY2026, only three are expected to be abolished; a Foreign Exchange Fund Special Account surplus is already earmarked for defense spending; and the Japan Business Federation opposes the remaining obvious option, a corporate tax hike. The secondary-market 10-year JGB yield has climbed from roughly 1.6% to near 3% since the cut was floated, and FY2027 interest payments are now projected at ¥16.59tn -- up ¥3.5tn from FY2026. Takaichi said Sept 23 she is eager to pass the bill; an extraordinary Diet session convenes Oct 5, where the funding question will be the central fight, with Takaichi having already ruled out deficit-financing bonds to cover the gap. **Trump and Bessent back a stronger yen (#121, Sept 25, 2026):** Katayama disclosed that Trump raised concern about yen weakness at the Sept 22 Takaichi summit; Takaichi said an undervalued yen is a problem. Bessent said he and Katayama discussed 'the desirability of a strong yen that reflects Japan's strong economic fundamentals' and agreed to stay in close communication. USD/JPY eased from 158.60 to ~158; 10Y JGB touched 3.115%, a ~30-year high. **40-year JGB auction strongest since 2020 (#123, Sept 29, 2026):** bid-to-cover 3.1 vs 2.82 at the July sale and a 2.67 12-month average; 40-year yield about 4.23% and JGB futures rose after the result. Demand attributed to yields above 4% drawing life insurers back to the super-long end, a week after the 10-year JGB broke above 3% in a global bond selloff. 2-year auction Sept 30 with yields near 2%. **Food tax cut goes to the Diet as October food prices rise on 3,153 items (#128, Oct 5, 2026):** The extraordinary Diet opened Oct 5 with the bill to cut the consumption tax on food from 8% to 1% for two years from April 2027 at the center of debate; the roughly ¥5tn annual cost still has no named funding source. Teikoku Databank counted 3,153 food and drink price increases for October and 20,187 for 2026, a second straight year above 20,000.

entities.name: METI (Ministry of Economy, Trade and Industry)
entities.desc: **AI regulation call and power-chip realignment (#130, Oct 2, 2026):** Minister Ryosei Akazawa announced, with the Digital Agency and Cabinet Office, a call (Oct 19-30) for laws, ordinances, notices and circulars that block deployment of LLMs, AI agents and physical AI such as AI robots, fully driverless vehicles and AI drones; METI will give hands-on support using the Industrial Competitiveness Enhancement Act's regulatory tools. At the same briefing he declined to comment on the stalled Rohm-Toshiba-Mitsubishi Electric power-chip merger but said METI will back domestic collaboration and realignment in power semiconductors. Japan's industrial policy ministry. Core AI infrastructure funder and semiconductor strategist. ¥1.23T AI/semiconductor budget envelope; ¥387.3B specifically for AI development. Backs Rapidus 2nm semiconductor project (~¥2.35T total government commitment). AI Promotion Act (AI推進法): enacted 2026, innovation-first, voluntary guidelines for most applications. **Genesis Mission (Issue #11, Jun 4–5, 2026):** Japan named first international partner in U.S. DOE Genesis Mission — $1B combined ($500M each) over 5 years; 12 U.S. national labs + 12 Japanese research institutions; quantum technology, nuclear fusion, biotechnology, materials AI, advanced manufacturing. MEXT co-sponsoring. **AI Basic Plan revision (Issue #22, Jun 20, 2026):** Draft revision released for public comment — adds enhanced international cooperation provisions and new cybersecurity plank on AI-enabled cyberattacks. Cabinet approval sought at early date; cybersecurity budget line likely to follow. **Noetra / ¥387.3B commitment (#31):** Largest single domestic AI commitment in Japan's history; ¥300B separately allocated to AI foundation models in FY2026 budget; Noetra's ¥387.3B exceeds prior NEDO AI programs by several multiples. **Revised AI Robotics Strategy (#32, Jul 1 2026):** 10 million AI-equipped robots across 18 sectors by 2040; gated on Noetra model readiness. **FSA AI compliance (#24):** Joint finalization of AI workflow guidelines effective July 1, 2026. **VTLA Dataset Consortium (#33, Jul 2 2026):** METI/NEDO solicitation selected Kawasaki+Fanuc+Yaskawa+Osaka University+FingerVision consortium to build VTLA physical-AI dataset — up to ¥2B over Aug 2026–Jul 2027. Goal: 5,000 hours of video, tactile, and motion data from automotive, robotics, and food-production sites; first multi-vendor standardized physical-AI training corpus in Japan. **Micron Hiroshima subsidy (#35, Jul 4 2026):** METI underwrote up to ¥536B of Micron's ¥1.5T Hiroshima HBM fab (groundbreaking Jul 4). Largest single semiconductor subsidy Japan has authorized; targets HBM supply for AI accelerators. **Japan AX / Second AI Basic Plan (#42, Jul 10 2026):** Prime Minister Takaichi's AI Strategy Headquarters adopted second-phase AI Basic Plan. Brands agenda "Japan AX" (日本AX). Two pillars: vertical AI (sector-specific models) + physical AI. 19 priority fields sorted by marketability, public value, and strategic importance. Orders cross-ministerial regulatory rewrite assuming AI is in the loop. AISI expanded to use frontier models for safety evaluation and cyber defense. Test: late-August FY2027 budget requests — dated line items per priority field determine whether plan has teeth. **Tower Semiconductor grant (#45, Jul 14 2026):** ~$1B in Japanese government grants supporting Tower's $3B silicon photonics + silicon-germanium expansion at Arai facility (300mm conversion). **¥370T economic-security investment blueprint (#81, Aug 11 2026):** The Takaichi Cabinet's long-term economic and fiscal policy guidelines target ¥370T ($2.3T) in combined public-private investment across 17 strategic sectors through fiscal 2040, with semiconductors and AI as the centerpiece alongside quantum, energy, biotech, and content. Sector detail includes ¥32.7T for data centers and storage batteries by FY2035. Unlike predecessor Ishiba's guidelines, the blueprint drops explicit 'fiscal consolidation' language in favor of 'stably' reducing the debt-to-GDP ratio over time. Ahead of the announcement, executives from Anthropic, TSMC, Microsoft, and Oracle met with the Takaichi government to make investment pitches — foreign frontier-AI and chip capacity now actively courting Japan's 17-sector spending envelope rather than the reverse. **Record ¥7.7T FY2027 budget request filed (#97, Sept 1, 2026):** METI submitted its fiscal 2027 budget request to the Finance Ministry on the Sept 1 government-wide deadline, seeking ¥7.7268 trillion — roughly 2.5x the prior year's request — with ¥4.525T of that under a new no-preset-ceiling investment quota and approximately ¥1.4T earmarked specifically for AI, semiconductor, and robotics initiatives. The request folds in the additional ¥150bn capital injection for Rapidus first flagged Aug 21, now a formal line item. METI's ask is one piece of a government-wide FY2027 budget request total approaching ¥130T across all ministries — a fourth consecutive record high — which the Finance Ministry will review ahead of Cabinet approval by year-end. The scale of the request is the clearest budget-cycle evidence yet of how far the Aug 11 ¥370T/17-sector economic-security blueprint has been translated into ministry-level spending asks. **$550B US investment pact: AI/chips to headline next tranche (#100, Sept 4, 2026):** Trade Minister Ryosei Akazawa told reporters in Washington that AI and semiconductor projects will carry 'very significant weight' in the next funding round of the Japan-US $550B investment framework, following meetings with US Commerce Secretary Howard Lutnick and USTR Jamieson Greer. Only $109B of the $550B has been committed after more than a year — $36B into US oil, gas, and mineral projects and $73B into a nuclear project spanning Tennessee/Alabama plus gas plants in Pennsylvania/Texas — and none of it into AI or chips yet. Akazawa declined to detail the third tranche. The structure caps direct equity at just 1-2% of the total, with the remainder as loans and guarantees through Japan's state-backed lenders (JBIC, NEXI) — meaning any AI/chip allocation would flow mostly as government-backed financing for US-based capacity rather than direct investment, a distinct channel from METI's domestic Rapidus/Kioxia subsidy programs tracked above. **HR development ecosystem project: Tokyo Electron selected for India training center (#114, Sept 19-20, 2026):** METI has selected Tokyo Electron to build a semiconductor HR-development-ecosystem hub in India, under which TEL will open a training center in Gujarat in 2027 to build a fab-engineer pipeline alongside local businesses and educational institutions. It's METI's workforce-side complement to its capital-heavy subsidy programs (Rapidus, Micron Hiroshima, Tower Semiconductor) — extending Japan's equipment-and-materials industrial-policy reach into human-capital formation for a foreign market, rather than only funding domestic capacity.

entities.name: Ministry of Justice (MOJ)
entities.desc: Japan's justice ministry. **Voice-rights interpretive guidance (#71, Aug 7, 2026):** Published a report — the output of a five-session expert study group running since April 2026 — stating that an individual's voice is already protected under existing Japanese law even without a dedicated statute: publicity rights (パブリシティー権, the exclusive right to commercially exploit the customer-drawing power of one's name or likeness) and personality-rights-derived protection against unwanted use (the 'right not to be used without cause,' みだりに利用されない権利) both extend to voice. Concretely, the MOJ said posting an unauthorized AI-cloned cover version of a singer's or voice actor's voice on social media for profit (AIカバー, 'AI cover') can constitute a publicity-rights violation — though ordinary human impressions or mimicry generally do not infringe. The guidance follows a wave of voice-actor complaints since AI voice-cloning tools proliferated from around 2023, including a lawsuit filed by voice actor Kenjiro Tsuda in November 2025 against a video-platform operator over an unauthorized AI-cloned video of his voice. No dedicated 'voice rights' statute yet exists — the report is interpretive guidance, not new legislation — but it gives claimants a clearer legal theory and puts platforms and AI voice-synthesis services on notice ahead of any future codification.

entities.name: NEDO
entities.zh: 新エネルギー・産業技術総合開発機構
entities.py: Shin-enerugī Sangyō Gijutsu Sōgō Kaihatsu Kikō
entities.desc: METI's innovation-funding agency — the clearest public map of where Japan's industrial-policy money flows. **Physical AI data infrastructure (Aug 2026):** NEDO awarded ¥2B to a Fanuc–Yaskawa–Kawasaki consortium (plus Osaka University and FingerVision) to build a cross-manufacturer tactile dataset — 5,000 hours of video, tactile, and motion data for a VTLA (Vision-Tactile-Language-Action) foundation model. Implementation period August 2026 – July 2027. The arrangement — three direct competitors agreeing to share factory floor data under a government mandate — is designed to give Japan's physical AI model (Noetra) training data advantages comparable to China's state-directed data pooling. **Other major bets:** ¥1tn Noetra foundation-model program; Hitachi–Intel–AIST silicon spin-qubit project (through March 2029).

tags.l: ¥2B tactile data: rivals pooling factory AI data (Aug 2026)

entities.name: Digital Agency (デジタル庁)
entities.desc: **Co-runs AI regulation-barrier call (#130, Oct 2, 2026):** With the Cabinet Office and METI, opened a request (submissions Oct 19-30 via a Cabinet Office form) for rules down to the level of notices and circulars that block AI deployment, explicitly covering AI agents and physical AI; Digital Minister Furukawa urged companies to respond. Results feed the Regulatory Reform Promotion Council and the next AI Basic Plan revision. Established 2021. Leads Japan's digital transformation. Government Gennai (ゲンナイ) generative AI platform launched nationwide May 2026 — government-wide AI deployment. **GENAI procurement guidelines Version 2.0 enter into force (#100, Sept 1, 2026):** The revised 'Guideline for the Procurement and Utilization of Generative AI for the Evolution and Innovation of Public Administration,' approved at the June 12 Council for the Promotion of a Digital Society meeting, took effect Sept 1. The update introduces mandatory Chief AI Officers at each ministry/agency to oversee deployment, procurement, data management, and risk; a structured high-risk-project assessment process requiring submission to the Advanced AI Utilization Advisory Board (objectives, mitigation measures, quality-assurance plans); and lifecycle governance requirements spanning model selection through decommissioning. The guidelines underpin a large-scale FY2026 pilot extending GENAI/Gennai access to roughly 180,000 government employees across all ministries, with full-scale rollout targeted from FY2027 — one of the largest government-wide generative AI deployments globally, and a governance template other agencies (and potentially private-sector regulators) may reference as AI procurement scales. **APPI Amendment (Issue #12, Jun 2026):** Personal Information Protection Act amendment passed lower house; removes individual consent requirement for AI training on medical histories and criminal records. Digital Minister Matsumoto Hisashi used 'AI colony' (AIの植民地) framing — data deregulation as national sovereignty issue. Bill in upper house debate; must clear before parliament rises July 2026. No civil-remedy mechanism — key risk. Primary beneficiaries if passes: healthcare AI, insurance underwriting, enterprise NLP. **APPI revision (#12, #30):** Bill cleared Lower House May 2026; Upper House vote before July 17 Diet recess; allows AI training on pseudonymized personal data without individual consent; Digital Agency / PPC joint review board. Primary beneficiary: Noetra physical AI consortium. **Data center siting (#23):** No MLIT/METI response to Chiba lawsuits as of June 2026; any zoning legislation requires prioritization before Diet recess.

tags.l: GENAI guidelines v2.0 in force; Chief AI Officers mandated (Sept 1)

entities.name: FSA (Financial Services Agency)
entities.desc: **AI data center financing review (#120, Sept 25, 2026):** Intensified scrutiny of banks' and life insurers' project-finance lending to AI data centers, mostly US-based, covering risk management, deal terms and related real-estate lending; officials cite uncertainty over hyperscaler returns but say the aim is vetting, not restriction. Japan's financial regulator. Launched public-private working group on AI-related cyber risks: 36 entities across 15 critical infrastructure sectors. Authorized Japan's three megabanks (MUFG, SMBC, Mizuho) to deploy dual AI cyber stack (Claude Mythos + OpenAI G-5.5). AI cyber governance framework in development. **AI workflow compliance guidelines (#24, #26, #30, Jun 22 2026):** Mandatory audit trails (監査証跡), explainability (説明可能性), and continuous model risk assessment for financial services, healthcare, energy, critical infrastructure. Three-month grace period ended July 1, 2026. Enforcement phase began July 1; examination findings expected Q3 2026 disclosures. Operationalizes AI Promotion Act (AI推進法, passed May 2025) into sector-specific mandates — first enforceable teeth in a major regulated sector. **Dedicated Crypto Assets and Stablecoins Division (#68, effective Aug 7 2026):** Elevated crypto and stablecoin oversight into a standalone division under the Asset Management and Insurance Supervision Bureau, consolidating responsibilities previously split across two units inside the Comprehensive Policy Bureau's Risk Analysis Office. The new division includes a Digital Asset Monitoring Office (exchange oversight), an Innovation Promotion Office, and a Digital Payment Planning Office. Framed as streamlining licensing/approvals for compliant exchanges and stablecoin issuers while sharpening scrutiny of market practices — organizational groundwork ahead of the FIEA amendment bill (Cabinet-approved April 2026) that would reclassify crypto assets as financial products, with implementation targeted as early as fiscal 2027, alongside a proposed flat 20% crypto tax rate. **Stablecoin cap removal (confirmed Aug 24, 2026):** Removed the ¥1,000,000 per-transaction ceiling on second-category Funds Transfer Service Providers (affecting JPYC), pairing the deregulation with the Crypto/Stablecoin Division's three offices (Crypto Asset Monitoring, Innovation Promotion, Digital Payment Planning) now operational to supervise the larger institutional flows the cap removal permits. Comprehensive stablecoin/custody framework still targeted for finalization by end-2026; contractor tax treatment and DeFi income rules remain unresolved. **2026 Strategic Priorities published, on-chain finance elevated to top policy category (Sept 15, 2026):** The FSA's 2026 Strategic Priorities name on-chain finance a top-tier category spanning payments, securities settlement, asset tokenization, and cross-border transfers. The agency will launch an "On-Chain Finance Forum for the AI Era" alongside a Study Group on Digital and Decentralized Finance and a Study Group on Promoting the Sound Use of AI and Related Technologies. The work operationalizes the Cabinet's July 2026 "Financial Strategy for Promoting Growth Investment," which named blockchain-based settlement as one of four strategic pillars. Four MUFG group companies began testing JGB repo transactions on the Canton Network in August under the FSA's Payment Innovation Project; an initial tokenized-settlement development plan is targeted for early 2027, with any operational system pushed into the 2030s.

entities.name: SB OAI Japan GK
entities.zh: SBオープンエーアイジャパン
entities.desc: OpenAI's Japan hub with SoftBank as the exclusive Japanese enterprise distribution partner. **SoftBank Enterprise exclusivity:** SoftBank has the right of first refusal for all enterprise ChatGPT/GPT API distribution to Japanese companies — a strategically important position as GPT-based workflows spread across Japan's corporate sector. **Government adoption:** Japan has been one of the most aggressive adopters of OpenAI tools among G7 governments; ministries and municipalities have piloted ChatGPT for document drafting and citizen services. **Tension with Noetra:** SoftBank simultaneously backs both SB OAI Japan (distributing US OpenAI products) and Noetra (developing Japan's sovereign AI model) — the two mandates eventually compete for the same enterprise wallet share; SoftBank's bet is that Japanese enterprises need both a sovereign model (for sensitive data) and a frontier US model (for general productivity).

entities.bio: SB OAI Japan GK is the legal entity for OpenAI's Japan operations, structured as a joint venture between SoftBank (JV partner and exclusive distribution partner) and OpenAI (founded 2015, San Francisco, by Sam Altman, Greg Brockman, Elon Musk and others). Established April 2024 in Tokyo. CEO of OpenAI Japan: Tadashi Nagata.

entities.name: PKSHA Technology
entities.desc: Japan's leading enterprise AI software company by revenue from domestic Japanese AI models. PKSHA's core business: licensing proprietary ML models to banks, insurers, and telecom operators for customer service automation, risk scoring, and recommendation systems. **PKSHA Algorithm License:** A recurring-license model for Japanese-language NLP that gives PKSHA stable revenue base before any single AI disruption event. **LARGE model push:** PKSHA has begun developing its own LLM foundation model for Japanese enterprise use, following the broader trend of Japanese AI companies shifting from narrow ML models to generative-AI-native architectures. Unlike Sakana AI or SB Intuitions (pure research/frontier bets), PKSHA is a revenue-generating enterprise AI software company — the most commercially grounded domestic Japanese AI company listed on the Tokyo Stock Exchange.
entities.bio: Founded 2012, Tokyo, by Shunsuke Aoki (CEO). Listed Tokyo Stock Exchange Prime Market (3993). Japan's leading 'algorithm' (AI/ML) company — provides AI models for natural language understanding, prediction, and recommendation to Japanese financial institutions, telecom operators, and enterprise clients.

entities.name: JIJ Inc.
entities.desc: Tokyo Tech spinout commercializing Professor Nishimori's quantum annealing research. Core customers: pharmaceutical and life sciences companies with complex scheduling/optimization problems (clinical trial scheduling, drug discovery pathway optimization, logistics routing). **Quantum-classical hybrid:** JIJ's approach runs quantum-inspired algorithms on classical hardware while integrating with actual quantum annealers (D-Wave, Fujitsu Digital Annealer) — hedging between quantum-only and classical-only solutions. In this landscape, JIJ represents Japan's academic-to-startup pipeline in deep-tech AI — a model that has produced fewer commercial successes in Japan than in the US or China, making each JIJ-style spinout commercially significant as a proof of concept.

entities.bio: Founded ~2020, Tokyo, by Yu Yamashiro (CEO and co-founder) — a graduate student spinout from Professor Hidetoshi Nishimori's quantum computing lab at Tokyo Institute of Technology (now Institute of Science Tokyo). Backed by several Japanese VCs. Core product: quantum-inspired and hybrid quantum-classical optimization algorithms for industrial scheduling problems.

entities.name: Mitsubishi Heavy Industries (MHI)
entities.desc: Japan's primary defense and aerospace industrial company, increasingly integrated with AI-driven autonomous systems. **H3 rocket and space AI:** MHI launches Japan's primary space launch vehicle (H3); JAXA collaboration on autonomous spacecraft and satellite constellations for Earth observation AI. **Defense AI:** MHI is Japan's primary integrator for JSDF (Japan Self-Defense Forces) weapons systems; the Ministry of Defense's AI-enhanced C4ISR (command, control, communications, computers, intelligence, surveillance, and reconnaissance) investments flow through MHI as the prime contractor. **Mitsubishi SpaceJet (MSJ):** The failed domestic aircraft development program (suspended 2023 after 15 years and ¥1T+ in losses) remains an open wound; MHI is applying lessons to its defense and heavy industry portfolio rather than consumer aviation. **NEC strategic alliance MOU (#99, Sept 2, 2026):** MHI and NEC signed an MOU to jointly develop command-and-control systems and unmanned-asset capabilities for Japan's Self-Defense Forces, explicitly framed around establishing 'data and AI sovereignty' as defense equipment and cloud operations increasingly integrate. CEO Eisaku Ito called it a foundation for 'a truly sovereign and highly reliable defense system' — the clearest signal yet that MHI, as Japan's prime defense contractor, is formalizing AI/data-sovereignty commitments alongside its traditional hardware role, rather than leaving that ground to IT-sector partners alone. **Preferred Networks capital alliance formalized (#114, Sept 16, 2026):** MHI is investing ¥10 billion in PFN via third-party allotment, converting the companies' June 2026 business tie-up into a capital alliance aimed at joint AI development for autonomous, mission-critical machinery and systems spanning social infrastructure and national security. Paired with the Sept 2 NEC MOU on C2 systems and unmanned assets, the PFN stake extends MHI's pattern of buying into AI-sovereignty partnerships — pairing balance-sheet capital with an outside model lab — rather than building frontier AI capability entirely in-house.

entities.bio: Founded 1884, Tokyo. CEO: Eisaku Ito. Listed TSE (7011). Japan's largest defense and heavy industry conglomerate; products span aircraft, naval vessels, rockets (H3 launch vehicle), energy systems, industrial machinery, and air conditioning. FY2024 revenue ~¥4.8T ($32B).

entities.name: Mitsubishi Electric
entities.desc: **Power-chip merger talks with Rohm and Toshiba stall (#130, Sept 30-Oct 2, 2026):** The March 27 basic agreement to merge power-semiconductor businesses under a likely holding company missed its summer target over equity ratios, business scope and leadership; the new goal is November interim results, with March 2027 as fallback. Mitsubishi Electric brings IGBT modules, Rohm SiC and Toshiba silicon MOSFETs; the combination would rank second globally behind Infineon. METI's Akazawa backed domestic realignment on Oct 2. Japan's leading industrial automation and building systems company, integrating AI into its Melsec factory automation platform. **PCI Energy Solutions acquisition (Aug 20):** Agreed to acquire the U.S. grid-optimization software firm for $1.4B (¥220B) — the largest acquisition in company history — betting that AI-driven data center power demand shifts the infrastructure bottleneck from chips to grid software; targets ¥200B in energy-solutions revenue and a 28% operating margin by FY2030. **AI-augmented Melsec:** Mitsubishi Electric's iQ-R series PLCs now integrate edge AI inference for predictive quality control and yield optimization — the AI upgrade path for the 2M+ Melsec controllers deployed globally. **SUCCESSOR humanoid (with Kawasaki):** Joint humanoid development project combining Kawasaki's robot motion hardware with Mitsubishi Electric's factory AI and sensing systems.

entities.name: Sakura Internet
entities.zh: さくらインターネット
entities.desc: Japan's domestically-built GPU cloud provider — the primary vehicle for METI's national AI computing subsidy program. **METI subsidy:** Received ¥501B ($3.4B) to build H100 GPU clusters for domestic AI training — by far the largest single Japanese government AI infrastructure commitment. **Domestic cloud alternative:** Positioned as a sovereignty-first alternative to US hyperscalers (AWS, Azure, GCP) for Japanese government and enterprise AI workloads involving sensitive data. **Utilization risk:** The key question is whether Japanese AI labs (Sakana AI, PKSHA, SB Intuitions/Noetra) and enterprise customers will use Sakura's GPU cloud rather than defaulting to US hyperscalers with superior global infrastructure and model ecosystems. Revenue in FY2024 was ~¥22B ($148M) — small relative to the subsidy scale; the subsidy is an investment in future capacity, not current earnings.
entities.bio: Founded 1996, Osaka, by Kuniaki Tasaka (田坂邦朗) and Junichi Ikeda. Listed TSE (3778). Japanese domestic cloud infrastructure provider; selected as METI's primary domestic AI computing subsidy recipient (¥501B allocated 2024–2025). CEO: Takahisa Kurahara.

entities.name: NTT Data
entities.desc: Japan's — and one of the world's — largest IT services companies, integrating AI across a massive enterprise and government client base. **AI-led development push (Aug 14, 2026):** Nikkei Asia reported NTT Data is among Japan's top systems integrators targeting a shift from people-led to AI-led software development by 2030 — using generative coding agents to compress the traditional requirements-design-build-test pipeline, a move that raises productivity but also shrinks the entry-level engineer headcount the industry has historically relied on. NTT Data and SoftBank anchor the 'OpenAI camp' of this transition (scale/innovation bet), a competitive split from the Fujitsu/NEC/Hitachi 'Anthropic camp' (security/reliability-first 'Japanese-style AI' positioning). **Japanese government AI integrator:** NTT Data is the primary systems integrator for Japan's national digital transformation agenda (MyNumber digital ID, government AI pilot programs, e-Gov). **Data-center buildout detailed, shares dip on capex concern (#98, Sept 4-5, 2026):** A Nikkei survey found Japan's AI data-center capacity on track to more than quadruple by 2033 on roughly $60bn of combined investment (NTT Data, Blackstone's $30bn pledge, and others). NTT Data's own share of that is ~750MW of new capacity by 2033, requiring an estimated ¥1.5tn ($9.6B) outlay (construction plus equipment, excluding Nvidia accelerators, at Japan's going rate of ¥2-2.5bn per installed MW). Near-term plans: 42MW added this year and a 100MW facility breaking ground in Tochigi Prefecture next year. NTT shares fell about 1% in Tokyo trading as Deepstone Partners CEO Yasuhiro Ono warned the capex could pressure the stock against deeper-pocketed global rivals. Global cloud providers (AWS, Microsoft) already drive over 80% of NTT Data's Japan data-center revenue, with capacity leasing out almost as fast as it's built — even as chronic grid-connection bottlenecks in hubs like Inzai, Chiba (8-10 years for regulatory/grid approval) push NTT Data toward utility partnerships (Tepco) and reinforce why rival SoftBank Corp is separately pursuing a direct equity stake in Tepco to secure power supply for its own AI buildout. **Generative AI services:** Launched 'iQuanta' generative AI consulting service (2024) and is deploying LLM-based workflow automation across its 190K+ global employees. **tsuzumi LLM:** NTT Group's proprietary Japanese-language LLM (tsuzumi) is distributed through NTT Data's enterprise relationships — a key differentiator vs. SoftBank (OpenAI distribution) and Fujitsu (Kozuchi).

entities.zh: コルト・テクノロジー・サービス
entities.desc: European/Asian private fiber network and cloud services company relevant to this landscape as a key network infrastructure provider for Japanese financial institutions' AI workloads. Colt's Japan operations connect Tokyo's major financial institutions (MUFG, Mizuho, SMBC) to global AI cloud platforms via private, low-latency fiber — a critical piece of the plumbing for AI-intensive trading, risk management, and compliance workloads. As financial institutions shift AI workloads to hyperscaler clouds, Colt's ability to provide private, compliant network access becomes a differentiator over public internet connectivity.

entities.bio: UK-based network and cloud services company, wholly owned by Fidelity Investments (US) since 2015. CEO: Carl Guildford. Operates a pan-European and Asian private fiber network; major Japan presence providing enterprise WAN and cloud connectivity to Japanese multinationals and financial institutions. Not a Japanese company.

entities.name: AIST
entities.desc: Japan's national applied-research institute under METI. Operates G-QuAT (Global Research and Development Center for Business by Quantum-AI Technology), a ~¥62bn (~$380M) quantum-AI facility hosting quantum and hybrid quantum-classical computing infrastructure. Named partner in the NEDO-backed Hitachi–Intel silicon spin-qubit project (July 2026), where it will co-build an open cloud platform giving external researchers remote access to experimental silicon quantum hardware and a fabrication ecosystem.
